docs.title: Open Data Framework
docs.text:
Lightweight dependency-injection framework for data applications.

Looking for the CLI, UI, MCP server, or chat?

Those live in the sibling odf package, which depends on this one. This site covers the core framework only — no UI, no CLI, no MCP server.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Most data projects end up solving the same structural problems repeatedly: how to wire dependencies, manage component lifecycles, and keep configuration separate from code. This framework provides that plumbing as a small set of reusable abstractions — Entity, Repository, Component, Service, Task, Pipeline, Agent, Function — so it doesn't need to be reinvented by hand in every project.

Want a ready-made project layout instead?

Scaffolding an actual project from a template is the odf package's job — this is what that scaffold is built on.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Install:

pip install opendataframework

A minimal project is a config file plus an app/ package:

.
├── config.toml
├── main.py
└── app/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── entities.py
    ├── repositories.py
    └── storages.py

app/entities.py — the data unit:

from dataclasses import dataclass

from opendataframework import Entity


@Entity
@dataclass
class User:
    id: int | None
    name: str

app/storages.py — a Component wired from config, doing the actual I/O:

import sqlite3

from opendataframework import Component, Config


@Component
class SQLite:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        self.conn = sqlite3.connect(config.component.sqlite.path)
        self.conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")

app/repositories.py — the Repository, depending on the storage:

from opendataframework import Repository

from app.entities import User
from app.storages import SQLite


@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def __init__(self, sqlite: SQLite) -> None:
        self.db = sqlite

    def all(self) -> list[User]:
        rows = self.db.conn.execute("SELECT id, name FROM users").fetchall()
        return [User(id=r[0], name=r[1]) for r in rows]

    def save(self, user: User) -> None:
        self.db.conn.execute("INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (?, ?)", (user.id, user.name))
        self.db.conn.commit()

Config file (config.toml):

[component.sqlite]
path = "app.db"

Main file (main.py):

from opendataframework import Project

from app.entities import User
from app.repositories import Users

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")
project.start()

users = project.context.get(Users)
users.save(User(id=None, name="Ada"))
print(users.all())

project.start() blocks until every component has completed its initialisation stage — there is no hidden latency on first access. Adding a new component means declaring its dependencies in the constructor, not writing wiring code — a config section is only needed if the component reads from Config itself.

Full lifecycle and usage patterns

See Project.

More worked, runnable projects

Each isolating exactly one core abstraction — see Examples.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Each concept below has a dedicated doc with the full interface, decorator usage, and worked examples.

Abstraction Role Entity Structured data unit (dataclass / ORM model) Repository Data access; manages Entities View Declares which representation and field(s) best fit a Repository's data Component DI-managed object with no execution contract Service Long-running Component (worker, backing service) Task Finite work unit; called explicitly Pipeline Ordered composition of Tasks/Pipelines Agent Goal-driven work unit whose steps are decided at run time; invoked with arguments Function Plain function made framework-aware; called by name with arguments Layer Decorator that assigns a registered class or function to a subsystem

Supporting the above are Context, Config, Project, Namespace, and Logger — the machinery that registers, resolves, and organises everything.

Machinery Role Context Registers, resolves, and lifecycles every component, in dependency order Config Wraps loaded TOML into the nested object components read via DI Project Composition root; owns the Context and starts/stops the application Namespace Base class behind every decorator (@Component, @Service, …); not an end-user concept Logger Per-component logging handle, injected already bound to its own class name

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
An Agent is a finite executable whose steps are decided at run time rather than written down in advance — typically by a language model working towards a goal it is handed when called. It is wired through dependency injection the same way as a Component, with a single invoke() contract that, unlike a Task's execute(), takes arguments.

The framework ships no model client and no agent loop. @Agent marks the place where one — an agentic library, a provider SDK, or hand-written logic — meets the rest of the project: its components, its configuration, its logging.

Agents answer one question:

What should work towards this goal, given what the project has?

docs.title: When to use Agent
docs.text:
Use @Agent when a class needs to:

  • be handed a goal at call time — a question, a ticket, a document
  • decide its own steps to reach it, usually by driving a model
  • act on the project's components, repositories, or services along the way
  • run to completion and return a result

Typical examples:

  • answering questions over a repository
  • triaging or classifying incoming records
  • drafting a report from several data sources
  • reviewing the output of a pipeline

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Agent decorator registers the class into the Agent namespace. The Context reads from this namespace at startup. The class is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Agent
class Librarian:
    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
@Agent(name="librarian")
class CatalogueAssistant:
    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
@Analytics
@Agent
class Librarian:
    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

invoke() is required

Applying @Agent to a class that does not define invoke() raises TypeError at decoration time, as does applying it to anything that is not a class.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
An Agent implements a single method — invoke(). Its signature is the author's to choose: any number of parameters, of any type, with or without defaults. It may return a value or None.

@Agent
class Librarian:
    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...


@Agent
class Triage:
    def invoke(self, ticket: Ticket, *, urgent: bool = False) -> Verdict: ...


@Agent
class NightlyReview:
    def invoke(self) -> Report: ...

No parameter name is reserved, and nothing in invoke() is injected — every parameter is supplied by the caller.

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Like all components, an Agent declares its dependencies through the constructor. For an agent this doubles as a statement of reach: what it can act on is exactly what its constructor asks for, and it shows up in the dependency graph like any other edge.

@Agent
class Librarian:
    def __init__(
        self,
        books: Books,
        model: Model,
        logger: Logger,
    ):
        self.books = books
        self.model = model
        self.logger = logger

    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

The model is usually one of those dependencies — a Component or Service of your own that holds the client and its configuration — so it can be shared between agents and replaced in tests.

docs.title: Using an Agent
docs.text:
An Agent is invoked through the Context by its key, agent.<name>, with keyword arguments passed on to invoke():

answer = project.context.call("agent.librarian", question="Anything by Herbert?")

Or by class, typed:

answer = project.context.get(Librarian).invoke("Anything by Herbert?")

project.context.parameters(Librarian) returns the parameters of invoke() — what a caller building a form or a schema needs to ask for.

Every invocation is logged to the agent's own log file — start, duration, and any exception — whichever way it was made. See Logger.

docs.title: As a step in a Pipeline
docs.text:
An agent is injected like any other dependency, so a Pipeline can make it one of its steps:

@Pipeline
class WeeklyDigest:
    def __init__(self, fetcher: NewBooksFetcher, librarian: Librarian):
        self.fetcher = fetcher
        self.librarian = librarian

    def execute(self):
        self.fetcher.execute()
        return self.librarian.invoke("Summarise this week's additions.")

docs.title: Functions as dependencies
docs.text:
What an agent may act on needn't be a class. A registered Function is declared in the constructor too, and arrives with its own dependencies filled in:

@Agent
class Librarian:
    def __init__(self, find: Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], find_titles], model: Model):
        self.find = find
        self.model = model

See Injecting a Function.

docs.title: Long-running agents
docs.text:
An agent is finite: one goal in, one result out. For an agent that works continuously — draining a queue, watching a stream — keep the loop in a Service and inject the agent into it:

@Service
class TicketWorker:
    def __init__(self, tickets: Tickets, triage: Triage):
        self.tickets = tickets
        self.triage = triage
        self._stopped = threading.Event()

    def setup(self): ...

    def run(self):
        while not self._stopped.is_set():
            for ticket in self.tickets.unprocessed():
                self.triage.invoke(ticket)
            self._stopped.wait(5)

    def stop(self):
        self._stopped.set()

docs.title: One agent using another
docs.text:
Agents can depend on each other through their constructors, with the same rule as everywhere else: no circular dependencies.

@Agent
class Editor:
    def __init__(self, librarian: Librarian): ...

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: An agent usually works by asking a language model, inside invoke(), what to do next. That makes "tool" mean two different things around an agent, declared in different places: the tools the agent uses while it works, and the tools it offers to a model somewhere else that wants to call it.

docs.title: Tools the agent uses
docs.text:
These are the agent's dependencies. Whatever it takes through its constructor — a component's methods, a registered function — is what it can hand to the model it runs inside invoke(). Nothing else is in reach, and the dependency graph shows it.

@Agent
class Librarian:
    def __init__(self, find: Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], find_titles], model: Model):
        self.model = model
        self.tools = {"find-titles": find}

    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

How those callables are described to the model is up to whatever runs the loop; an injected function keeps its name and docstring, and its signature lists only the arguments a caller supplies.

This half needs nothing beyond this package.

docs.title: Tools the agent offers
docs.text:
A model outside the agent — a chat assistant, an MCP client — can call it only if something serves the project's tools to that model. This package doesn't: it has no MCP server, and here an agent is invoked by project code alone, through a class that injects it or through project.context.call().

The agent itself needs no declaration to be offered. A server built on the framework can find every resolved agent through the Context and offer its invoke(), described by the class docstring, with project.context.parameters(Librarian) as the arguments to ask for. So the docstring and the parameters of invoke() are what the calling model sees. The parameters should be types a schema can express, like a str, a number or a dataclass, not an arbitrary object.

@Agent
class Librarian:
    """Answers questions about the book catalogue."""

    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

To offer more than invoke(), for example a narrower, cheaper method beside it, the agent implements mcp_tools() like any other class (see Component → MCP Tools). Don't name one of those tools invoke, because a server that offers the agent's invoke() already uses that name:

@Agent
class Librarian:
    """Answers questions about the book catalogue."""

    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str: ...

    def titles(self, author: str) -> list[str]: ...

    def mcp_tools(self) -> list[McpTool]:
        return [
            McpTool(
                name="titles",
                description="List the catalogue's titles by an author.",
                handler=self.titles,
            )
        ]

Seeing it in practice

The sibling odf package's McpServer offers every resolved agent as <key>.invoke and every mcp_tools() entry as <key>.<name>, so the model on the other side sees agent.librarian.invoke and agent.librarian.titles. When it calls invoke, the librarian uses the tools from its constructor to work out the answer.

The two are independent. An agent that uses tools needn't offer any beyond invoke(), and one that offers several needn't use any.

docs.title: Wrapping an agentic library
docs.text:
invoke() is where a library's own agent runs. The class holds it, hands it the project's components as tools, and exposes one method to the framework. The example below uses Pydantic AI, which is not a dependency of this package — any library, or none, fits the same shape.

from pydantic_ai import Agent as ModelAgent


@Agent
class Librarian:
    """Answers questions about the book catalogue."""

    def __init__(self, books: Books, config: Config):
        self.books = books
        self.agent = ModelAgent(
            config.agent.librarian.model, instructions="Answer from the catalogue."
        )
        self.agent.tool_plain(self.find)

    def find(self, title: str) -> list[str]:
        """Find books whose title contains the given text."""
        return [book.title for book in self.books.search(title)]

    def invoke(self, question: str) -> str:
        return self.agent.run_sync(question).output

For a version with no third-party dependency at all — a rule-based stand-in for the model, so the loop itself is visible — see examples/09-agent/.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
AgentProtocol documents the expected interface and is available for type checking and introspection:

from opendataframework import AgentProtocol

isinstance(instance, AgentProtocol)  # True if invoke() is present

AgentProtocol is @runtime_checkable, so the check confirms only that invoke is present, not its signature.

class AgentProtocol(Protocol):
    def invoke(self, *args, **kwargs): ...

docs.title: What Agent is Not
docs.text:
• Not a model client. The framework has no third-party dependencies and talks to no provider. The model is a dependency you supply.

  • Not an agent loop. Planning, tool calling, retries, and memory belong to the library or code inside invoke().

  • Not a long-running process. invoke() runs to completion. For continuous work, inject the agent into a Service.

  • Not async, and not streamed for you. The Context calls and never awaits, so an async def invoke() makes project.start() raise TypeError. An invoke() that returns an iterator hands it back as is; the log then records when the iterator was created, not how long it took to finish.

  • Not a base class. Librarian does not inherit from Agent. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: I need to... Use Provide a reusable capability Component Run a process indefinitely Service Execute a bounded unit of work once, no arguments Task Call a unit of work with arguments Function Coordinate multiple tasks into a workflow Pipeline Work towards a goal handed over at call time Agent Manage persistent data Repository

docs.title: Component
docs.text:
A Component is a Python class registered in the Component namespace via the @Component decorator — the foundational building block of the framework. Decorating a class with @Component is what makes it participate in dependency injection; the Context reads this namespace at startup to build the dependency graph and create instances.

Component carries no execution contract. It does not require specific methods to be implemented. Its role is to be wired into the system, receive its dependencies through the constructor, and provide whatever capability it encapsulates.

docs.title: When to use Component
docs.text:
Use @Component when a class provides a reusable capability that:

  • does not need to run indefinitely (that is a Service)
  • does not execute a single bounded unit of work (that is a Task)
  • does not coordinate other tasks (that is a Pipeline)
  • does not work towards a goal handed over at call time (that is an Agent)
  • does not manage the entities of one data source (that is a Repository)

If none of the above apply, it is a Component.

Typical examples:

  • a model wrapper (fit, predict)
  • a data validator
  • a feature transformer
  • a notification sender
  • a configuration reader
  • a client wrapper around an external API

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Component decorator registers the class into the Component namespace at definition time and marks it for dependency injection and lifecycle participation. The class itself is returned unchanged — no base class is added, no methods are injected.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Component
class Classifier:
    def fit(self, data): ...

    def predict(self, data): ...

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
An optional name can be provided to register the component under something shorter than the kebab-case form of its class name — useful when the class name is long and you'd rather look it up by a short alias via Component.get(...).

@Component(name="churn-risk")
class CustomerChurnRiskClassifier:
    def fit(self, data): ...

    def predict(self, data): ...

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
@Component is often stacked with a layer decorator to indicate which subsystem the component belongs to. Layer comes first (outermost), component type second — a class takes one execution type, so @Component is not combined with @Service, @Task and the like (see Namespace):

@Analytics
@Component
class Classifier:
    def fit(self, data): ...

    def predict(self, data): ...

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Dependencies are declared through the constructor. The Context resolves and injects them automatically when the component is created.

@Analytics
@Component
class Report:
    def __init__(
        self,
        classifier: Classifier,
        metrics: Metrics,
    ):
        self.classifier = classifier
        self.metrics = metrics

    def build(self, data):
        prediction = self.classifier.predict(data)
        self.metrics.save(prediction)
        ...

No service locators. No imports of global registries. The constructor signature is the complete and readable description of what this component needs.

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
A realistic component in a data analytics project:

@Analytics
@Component
class Classifier:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
        metrics: Metrics,
    ):
        self.config = config.component.classifier
        self.metrics = metrics
        self.model = self._load_model(self.config.model_path)

    def fit(self, data):
        self.model.fit(data)
        self.metrics.save_training_run(data)

    def predict(self, data):
        return self.model.predict(data)

    def _load_model(self, path): ...

docs.title: Namespace
docs.text:
Component is a namespace — a named scope that maps registration names to classes. Two class methods are available for inspection:

Component.get("Classifier")  # → Classifier class, or None if not registered
Component.get("metrics-classifier")  # → Classifier class registered under a custom name

dict(Component.items())  # → {"classifier": Classifier, ...}

get() accepts any name form

.get() normalizes its argument before looking it up, so PascalCase ("Classifier"), snake_case ("metrics_fetcher"), and kebab-case ("metrics-fetcher") all resolve to the same registration — that's why Component.get("Classifier") finds a class stored under the kebab-case key "classifier".

The Context uses these to discover registered components at startup. Application code does not call them directly.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
A Component may optionally implement details() to surface key/value information about itself — a running service's URL, a port it bound, a dashboard link. It is independent of on_start()/on_stop() and is never called by the Context; it's detected structurally and called on demand by whatever's inspecting the component, so values that only exist after startup are reflected rather than frozen at resolve time.

@Api
@Service
class Dashboard:
    def __init__(self, config: Config):
        self.port = config.service.dashboard.port

    def details(self) -> dict[str, str]:
        return {"UI": f"http://localhost:{self.port}"}

details() is detected structurally via DetailsProtocol (opendataframework.component.DetailsProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required:

class DetailsProtocol(Protocol):
    def details(self) -> dict[str, str]: ...

A component with no details() method simply has nothing to surface here — this is entirely optional.

Seeing it in practice

The sibling odf package's UI has a Details button in its object inspector; clicking it calls details() on demand, via GET /api/components/{id}/details, and shows the result. That's just today's one consumer, though — nothing here depends on it.

docs.title: Chart
docs.text:
A Component may optionally implement chart() to render a custom visualization, backed by whatever Python charting library it likes (matplotlib, plotly, ...) rather than requiring a JS charting library on the consumer's side. Like details(), it is independent of on_start()/on_stop() and is never called by the Context — it's detected structurally and called on demand by whatever's inspecting the component, so the chart reflects live repository state on every call rather than being frozen at resolve time.

chart() must return a self-contained HTML document — inline image/JS, no external file references — so a caller can embed it safely:

@Analytics
@Component
class UsersByStore:
    def __init__(self, users: Users, stores: Stores):
        self.users = users
        self.stores = stores

    def chart(self) -> str:
        fig = ...  # build a matplotlib/plotly/... figure from self.users, self.stores
        return f"<html><body><img src='data:image/png;base64,{encoded}'></body></html>"

Because the chart lives on a normal DI-managed Component, it gets constructor-injected access to repositories and other components just like any other component — no separate data-fetching layer is needed.

chart() is detected structurally via ChartProtocol (opendataframework.component.ChartProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required:

class ChartProtocol(Protocol):
    def chart(self) -> str: ...

A component with no chart() method simply has no chart to show — this is entirely optional.

Seeing it in practice

The sibling odf package's UI calls chart() on demand, per request to GET /api/components/{id}/chart, serves the returned string as text/html, and renders it inside a same-origin <iframe> — which is why the HTML must be self-contained. That's just today's one consumer, though — nothing here depends on it.

docs.title: MCP Tools
docs.text:
A Component may optionally implement mcp_tools() to expose its own custom MCP tools, in addition to the fixed lifecycle/task/pipeline surface. Like details()/chart(), it is independent of on_start()/on_stop() and is never called by the Context — it's detected structurally and consumed on demand by whatever builds an MCP tool surface.

@Component
class Weather:
    def __init__(self, config: Config):
        self.api_key = config.component.weather.api_key

    def forecast(self, city: str) -> dict: ...

    def mcp_tools(self) -> list[McpTool]:
        return [
            McpTool(
                name="forecast",
                description="Get the weather forecast for a city.",
                handler=self.forecast,
            )
        ]

mcp_tools() is detected structurally via McpToolsProtocol (opendataframework.component.McpToolsProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required:

class McpToolsProtocol(Protocol):
    def mcp_tools(self) -> list[McpTool]: ...

Each returned McpTool carries a name, description, handler (a callable — usually a bound method), and structured_output flag. A component with no mcp_tools() method simply exposes no custom tools — this is entirely optional.

Whoever calls a tool — typically a model — sees only its description and the handler's signature, so an McpTool checks both when it is created:

  • the description is not empty — ValueError otherwise;
  • every parameter of the handler is annotated;
  • the handler takes no *args or **kwargs;
  • the handler has a return annotation (-> None counts);
  • no annotation is a string — as every one is under from __future__ import annotations.

A handler that falls short raises TypeError, naming the tool and everything that is missing. A lambda has no annotations, so it can't be a handler — use a method or a function.

Because detection is structural, any class the Context creates can provide tools this way — a Repository, a Service, a Task, an Agent — not only a @Component.

docs.title: A function as a tool
docs.text:
A handler needn't be a method. A registered Function the class takes through its constructor arrives with its own dependencies filled in and a signature that leaves them out, so it can be returned as a handler directly:

@Function
def find_titles(catalogue: Catalogue, author: str) -> list[str]:
    """Find the titles the catalogue holds by an author."""
    return catalogue.titles_by(author)


@Component
class Library:
    def __init__(self, find: Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], find_titles]):
        self.find = find

    def mcp_tools(self) -> list[McpTool]:
        return [
            McpTool(
                name="find-titles",
                description="Find the titles the catalogue holds by an author.",
                handler=self.find,
            )
        ]

The tool asks for author only. Returning it from a class lets the tool take its own name and description, and sit beside the class's other tools. See Injecting a Function.

Seeing it in practice

This package only defines the McpTool/McpToolsProtocol shape — it has no MCP server of its own. The sibling odf package's McpServer is the consumer: it registers each returned McpTool under <key>.<tool.name> (component.weather.forecast), next to its six fixed built-in tools. It also offers every resolved Agent as <key>.invoke and every registered Function as <key>.call without any mcp_tools(), so a tool returned here must not reuse one of those names.

docs.title: What Component is Not
docs.text:
• Not a base class. Classifier does not inherit from Component. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

  • Not an execution unit. The framework does not call any method on a Component automatically — it is instantiated and wired, nothing more. If you need the framework to call run() or execute(), use Service or Task instead.

  • Not created more than once. The Context creates exactly one instance per registered class and returns that same instance from every context.get(cls) call — see Context.

docs.text: I need to... Use Provide a reusable capability Component Run a process indefinitely Service Execute a bounded unit of work once, no arguments Task Call a unit of work with arguments Function Coordinate multiple tasks into a workflow Pipeline Work towards a goal handed over at call time Agent Manage persistent data Repository

docs.title: Config
docs.text: Config is the framework's configuration abstraction. It wraps a nested dictionary — typically loaded from TOML — and exposes it through attribute and item access with automatic name normalisation. Components that need configuration declare config: Config as a constructor dependency and receive it via DI.

docs.title: From a file
docs.text: project = Project.from_config("config.toml")

docs.title: From a directory
docs.text:
All *.toml files in the directory are loaded in alphabetical order and deep-merged. Later files override earlier ones for scalar values; nested dicts are merged recursively.

project = Project.from_config("config/prod/")

A typical layout:

config/
├── analytics.toml
├── api.toml
├── data.toml
└── storage.toml

docs.title: From a dict
docs.text:
Primarily for testing or programmatic configuration:

project = Project.from_dict(
    {"component": {"postgres": {"database-url": "postgresql://localhost/mydb"}}}
)

docs.title: Receiving config in a component
docs.text:
Any component that declares config: Config in its constructor receives the full project config automatically:

from opendataframework import Component, Config


@Component
class Postgres:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        self.url = config.component.postgres.database_url

By convention it reads its own section, [component.postgres] — see Config structure convention.

Only components that need configuration have to declare this dependency. Components that do not need it simply omit it.

docs.title: Attribute access
docs.text:
Both snake_case and kebab-case names are accepted interchangeably:

database-url = "postgresql://localhost/mydb"

config.database_url  # "postgresql://localhost/mydb"
config["database-url"]  # same

This works in both directions: keys in the file are normalised too, so database_url = "..." in TOML is found by config.database_url, config["database-url"] and config.get("database_url") alike. Two keys in the same table that normalise to the same name (e.g. database_url and database-url) raise a ValueError rather than one silently winning.

docs.title: Nested sections
docs.text:
Accessing a key whose value is a dict returns a nested Config object, so access can be chained:

[component.postgres]
database-url = "postgresql://localhost/mydb"
port = 5432

A dotted TOML header is a table inside a table, so this is reached in two steps:

config.component.postgres.database_url
config["component"]["postgres"]["port"]

docs.title: Safe access with get()
docs.text:
Config.get(key, default) returns the value at key, or default if the key is absent. It does not raise:

config.get("host", "localhost")  # "localhost" if key absent

get() and [] normalize the key too

normalize() runs on every access path — attribute, [], and get() alike. For a [component.postgres] TOML section, config.component.postgres, config["component"]["postgres"], and config.get("Component").get("Postgres") all find it.

If default is omitted and the key is absent, get() returns an empty Config rather than None. This makes scoping into a section safe by default — a component can grab its own slice of the config and chain further access onto it without guarding against the section being missing:

cfg = config.get("component").get("postgres")

cfg.database_url  # AttributeError if missing
cfg.get("port", 5432)  # 5432 if key absent

This lets each component retrieve its own slice without coupling it to the full config structure, while leaving the full config accessible for cross-cutting needs:

@Component
class Postgres:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        cfg = config.component.postgres
        self.url = cfg.database_url
        self.pool_size = cfg.get("pool-size", 10)


@Component
class Observability:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        cfg = config.component.observability
        self.log_level = cfg.get("log-level", "INFO")
        # reads another component's section too
        self.database_url = config.component.postgres.database_url

docs.title: Config structure convention
docs.text:
The framework imposes no required structure on the config file. By convention, a class reads the section named after its key, <namespace>.<name> — the same key the Context addresses it by and its log file is named after. A @Service class Postgres reads [service.postgres], an @Repository(User) class Users reads [repository.users]:

[service.postgres]
database-url = "postgresql://localhost/mydb"
pool-size = 10

[service.users-api]
host = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8080

[repository.users]
table = "users"
schema = "public"

@Service
class Postgres:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        cfg = config.service.postgres
        ...

A name is unique only within its namespace, so the namespace keeps two same-named classes apart here too: a @Task class Loader reads [task.loader] and an @Agent class Loader reads [agent.loader].

This convention is not enforced — components access whatever key they declare in their constructor, and nested sections remain reachable via chained .get()/attribute access (e.g. config.get("outer").get("inner")) if a project's config genuinely needs them. Using the key consistently makes config files predictable and easy to navigate, and means a class has one name everywhere: [service.postgres] in config, Context.start("service.postgres"), logs/service.postgres.log. The section moves with the namespace — changing @Component to @Service moves [component.postgres] to [service.postgres]. It is independent of Layer, which is an organisational grouping and has no bearing on config structure.

Same convention, everywhere

The sibling odf package's UI and CLI also address components by this same key. It's a convention, not something Config enforces — but since every access path normalizes casing, config.service.postgres finds the section however the TOML header itself is cased.

docs.title: The [project] section is reserved
docs.text:
Unlike every other section (which is a convention, not enforced), [project] is read directly by Project.from_config()/Project.from_dict() itself, before any Config object exists — so its keys must be written exactly as shown, not normalized like the accessors above:

[project]
log-dir = "logs"   # see Logger
app = "app"        # see Project — imports the app package

See Project and Logger for what each key does.

docs.title: What Config is Not
docs.text:
• Not a validator. Config does not validate types, required fields, or value ranges. Validation is the component's own responsibility.

  • Not injectable into every component automatically. Only components that explicitly declare config: Config in their constructor receive it. Components that do not need configuration simply omit the parameter.

  • Not mutable. Config provides read-only access. Configuration is set at project creation time and does not change at runtime. Config deep-copies the dict it's given at construction time, so mutating a dict you passed to Project.from_dict() after the fact has no effect on the Config a component already received.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Context is the framework's dependency-injection and lifecycle engine. It manages the full lifecycle of application components — registering them, resolving their dependencies, creating instances in the correct order, and coordinating startup and shutdown.

Everything the framework does flows through the Context. Project owns it and exposes project.context.get(cls) to fetch any resolved instance by its class.

Minimal, self-contained example

Any registered class works — here's a plain Component, defined and fetched:

@Component
class Classifier:
    def predict(self, data): ...


project = Project.from_config("config.toml")
project.start()

classifier = project.context.get(Classifier)
classifier.predict(data)

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
Responsibility Description Registration Tracks all classes and functions declared with framework decorators Dependency resolution Builds the dependency graph from constructor signatures Instance creation Creates instances in dependency order Lifecycle management Drives the lifecycle of every component in the correct order

Registration is global; instances are per-Context

Every class registered with a framework decorator becomes part of the shared namespace the moment its module is imported — every Project's Context instantiates it, regardless of that project's config. A [section] in config.toml only supplies values a constructor reads via config: Config; it doesn't determine which classes get built. What isn't shared is state: each Project owns its own Context, so its instances stay separate from any other Project in the same process.

[project] app controls import timing, not scope

[project] app = "app" in config.toml just runs importlib.import_module("app") before the Context resolves — equivalent to writing import app by hand before Project.from_config()/Project.from_dict() is called. It doesn't create a new per-Project component-isolation mechanism: the global-registration behavior described above still fully applies — once a module is imported (by this key or by any other means), every Project's Context in the process can see the classes it registers. See Project.

docs.title: How it Works
docs.text:
The Context operates as an internal engine — components are registered via decorators at class definition time, and the Context does the rest when the Project starts. Most end users never interact with it directly.

Decorators register components at definition time
    → @Component, @Service, @Task, @Pipeline, @Agent, @Repository, @Function

project.start() triggers context initialisation
    → Context builds the dependency graph from constructor signatures
    → For each component in dependency order:
        → if Service:                     setup() → run() (backgrounded by framework)
        → if Component/Repository defines on_start(): called directly, blocking
        → otherwise:                      instantiated only
    → project.start() returns — everything is ready

project.stop() triggers context teardown
    → For each component in reverse dependency order:
        → if Service:                     stop() (signals background thread to exit)
        → if Component/Repository defines on_stop(): called directly, blocking
        → otherwise:                      no teardown

docs.title: Dependency Graph
docs.text:
The Context derives the dependency graph automatically from constructor signatures. No explicit dependency declarations are needed.

@Api
@Service
class UsersApi:
    def __init__(self, users: Users):
        self.users = users


@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def __init__(self, postgres: Postgres):
        self.postgres = postgres


@Storage
@Service
class Postgres:
    def __init__(self, config: Config):
        self.config = config

The Context resolves the full graph:

Config      ← no dependencies, initialised first
    ↓
Postgres    ← depends on Config
    ↓
Users       ← depends on Postgres
    ↓
UsersApi    ← depends on Users

A registered Function is part of the same graph. It depends on the managed types in its signature, and a class depends on it by naming it in Annotated[..., func] — see Injecting a Function. It is bound in dependency order alongside the classes, but has no lifecycle and is not in context.instances.

One of each

The Context holds a single instance of every class, so asking for the same one twice — def __init__(self, source: Db, target: Db) — would hand over the same object under both names. That raises ValueError at project.start(), naming the class, the dependency and the parameters. If two are needed, register two classes.

docs.title: Startup Order
docs.text:
Startup runs in dependency order — dependencies first, dependents after.

For each component, the framework applies the appropriate lifecycle:

Postgres
    → setup()             ← Service lifecycle, blocking
    → run()               ← backgrounded by framework, continues to next

Users
    → instantiated        ← Repository (no on_start() defined here)

UsersApi
    → setup()             ← Service lifecycle, blocking
    → run()               ← backgrounded by framework

project.start() blocks until all components have completed their initialisation stage. After it returns, everything is ready — no hidden latency, no partial state.

Config isn't part of this walk

Config isn't decorated with @Component and isn't registered in any namespace, so it's never collected into the dependency-ordered list above. Project/Context construct it upfront and seed it directly into the resolved instances, before dependency resolution even starts — it's simply already there for anything that declares config: Config to receive, with no lifecycle of its own.

Readiness — do setup work inside setup()

Services should complete all setup work inside setup(). The framework waits for setup() to return before proceeding to the next component, so any service that opens connections or runs migrations in setup() is guaranteed to be ready before dependents start.

Component/Repository startup hook

If Users (or any Component/Repository) defines on_start(), it's called at this same point in dependency order, blocking, right where "instantiated" appears above. It's optional and independent of on_stop() — see Repository for the full pattern (connections, file handles, and similar lightweight setup that should happen once, at Project start).

docs.title: Shutdown Order
docs.text:
Shutdown runs in reverse dependency order — dependents are stopped before their dependencies.

UsersApi    → stop()      ← Service stopped first
Users       → (none)      ← Repository (no on_stop() defined here)
Postgres    → stop()      ← Service stopped last

This ensures no component is stopped while something that depends on it is still running.

Config isn't part of this walk either

Just as in Startup Order, Config was never collected into the dependency-ordered list, so it doesn't appear above at all — unlike Users, which is listed with (none) because it is part of the walk but simply has no on_stop() to call.

Component/Repository shutdown hook

If Users (or any Component/Repository) defines on_stop(), it's called at this same point in reverse dependency order, blocking.

docs.title: Circular Dependencies
docs.text:
Circular dependencies indicate a design problem and are not supported. If A depends on B and B depends on A, the Context cannot determine a valid initialisation order.

Raises ValueError

Detecting a cycle raises ValueError, naming the classes — and any functions — involved: Circular dependency detected among: A, B. This surfaces at project.start(), not at class-definition time — decorators only register classes, they don't check the graph.

The fix is to introduce a third collaborator that both can depend on, or replace one of the dependencies with an event or callback:

# problem
class A:
    def __init__(self, b: B): ...


class B:
    def __init__(self, a: A): ...  # circular


# solution — extract shared concern into C
class A:
    def __init__(self, c: C): ...


class B:
    def __init__(self, c: C): ...

docs.title: Direct Access
docs.text:
project.context.get(cls) fetches any resolved instance by its class — the intended entry point for top-level application code, scripts, and notebooks:

users = project.context.get(Users)
users.all()

project.context.instances is the lower-level, untyped dict backing get() — primarily useful for framework extension authors:

# use the context directly — useful in extensions and tooling
with project.context as ctx:
    component = ctx.instances[UsersApi]

get(cls) relies on every registered class being a per-Context singleton — exactly one instance per class, stored in instances. Logger is the one constructor dependency that breaks this: it isn't registered in any namespace and has no slot in instances at all, so context.get(Logger) doesn't work — see Logger.

get() also accepts a registered Function, returning it with its managed dependencies already filled in:

load = project.context.get(load_data)
load("data.csv")  # db injected

Functions are kept out of instances — that mapping holds classes only. project.context.functions is the equivalent for functions (function → bound callable), and project.context.parameters(func) returns the parameters a caller still has to supply. See Function.

docs.title: By Key — Single-Component Control
docs.text:
Beyond get(cls), Context exposes a control surface addressed by key — every method below takes <namespace>.<name>, where <name> is the name the object is registered under (its kebab-case class or function name, or the explicit name=):

Registered as Key @Service class Postgres "service.postgres" @Repository(Frame) class Webcam "repository.webcam" @Pipeline class DailyAnalytics "pipeline.daily-analytics" @Task("export") class ExportUsers "task.export" @Function def load_data "function.load-data" @Agent class Librarian "agent.librarian"

A name is unique only within its namespace, so the namespace is always part of the key: a @Task class Loader and an @Agent class Loader can live in the same project as "task.loader" and "agent.loader". Keys are accepted in any casing ("Task.LoadJob" is "task.load-job"). A string without a namespace raises ValueError, and a key that matches no resolved object raises KeyError. project.context.key(obj) returns the key of a class or function you already hold:

project.context.key(DailyAnalytics)  # → "pipeline.daily-analytics"

This is the mechanism a UI, CLI, or MCP server built on top of the framework uses to control one component at a time without importing its class:

Services — start, stop, or check a single Service independent of the normal dependency-order startup/shutdown driven by project.start()/ project.stop():

project.context.start("service.postgres")  # no-op if already running
project.context.stop("service.postgres")  # no-op if not running
project.context.is_running("service.postgres")  # → bool

Each raises TypeError if the matched instance isn't a Service.

Streams — start, stop, check, or attach to a StreamableProtocol repository's background stream (see Repository):

project.context.start_stream("repository.webcam")  # spawns the background thread
project.context.stop_stream("repository.webcam")  # no-op if not streaming
project.context.is_streaming("repository.webcam")  # → bool

for frame in project.context.iter_stream("repository.webcam"):
    ...  # one subscriber; detaches when the stream stops or iteration ends

start_stream()/stop_stream() mirror start()/stop() for services and raise TypeError if the matched instance isn't StreamableProtocol. iter_stream() only attaches to an already-running stream — it doesn't start one itself, and raises KeyError if the stream isn't currently running.

Tasks and Pipelines — execute a single resolved Task or Pipeline:

project.context.execute("pipeline.daily-analytics")  # → whatever execute() returns

Raises TypeError if the matched instance is neither.

Functions — call a single resolved Function. Unlike execute(), call() forwards arguments: the Context fills in the parameters whose type it manages, and the keywords supply the rest:

project.context.call("function.load-data", path="data.csv")  # db injected

Raises TypeError if a required argument is neither managed nor supplied.

Agents — call() also invokes a single resolved Agent, passing the keywords on to its invoke(). An agent's dependencies were already injected through its constructor, so every keyword here is one of invoke()'s own arguments:

project.context.call("agent.librarian", question="Anything by Herbert?")

A function and an agent may share a name — "function.librarian" and "agent.librarian" are different keys.

project.context.parameters(target) returns what a caller must supply to call() — a function's parameters minus the injected ones, or the parameters of an agent's invoke().

Logs — read back a component's recent log lines (see Logger); each key has its own <namespace>.<name>.log file:

project.context.tail_logs("service.postgres", lines=300)
# → [{"ts": ..., "level": ..., "message": ...}, ...], oldest first

docs.title: What Context is Not
docs.text:
• Not a service locator for internal wiring. Components should declare dependencies through their constructor, not look them up from the Context at runtime — project.context.get(cls) is for top-level and cross-cutting access, not a replacement for dependency injection between components.

  • Not directly called by end users during startup. Registration and wiring happen through decorators and constructor signatures; the Context resolves and drives lifecycle as an internal engine. project.context.get(cls) is the entry point end users reach for only after project.start() returns — and even then, it's not something that should be used directly in most cases: most dependency logic belongs inside a class that receives it via constructor injection, not in code that pulls it from the Context directly.

  • Not async. The Context calls and never awaits. An async def in anything it would call — a Function, execute(), invoke(), setup()/run()/ stop(), on_start()/on_stop(), a repository's stream methods — makes project.start() raise TypeError naming it, before anything is created. Other async def methods on a component are yours to call and are left alone.

  • Not a reader of string annotations. Dependencies are injected by type, and an annotation that is a string is not one — every annotation is, under from __future__ import annotations. A required constructor parameter left unfilled for that reason raises a TypeError that says so; remove the import, or the quotes around the annotation.

  • Not responsible for threading. The framework handles Service.run(), and a streamable Repository's stream(), in background threads automatically. Neither the service/repository author nor the context caller needs to manage this directly.

docs.title: Entity
docs.text:
An Entity is a named, structured unit of data that the system passes around. It represents a meaningful piece of information in the domain — a database record, a configuration object, a sensor reading, a video frame, or any other structured data that components, repositories, and pipelines work with.

Entities answer one question:

What does the data look like?

Not where it comes from or how it is processed — that's a Repository's job. Entities are the common language of the application.

docs.title: When to use Entity
docs.text:
Use @Entity when a class represents a structured unit of data that:

  • is passed between components, tasks, or pipelines
  • has a well-defined shape that the rest of the system depends on
  • represents a domain concept worth naming explicitly

Typical examples:

  • a user record
  • an order
  • a sensor reading
  • a metric snapshot
  • a video frame
  • a configuration record

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Entity decorator registers the class with the framework as a data structure. It is a marker — the class is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Entity
@dataclass
class User:
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
An optional name can be provided to register the entity under something other than the kebab-case form of its class name — useful when the class name doesn't match the domain name you want to look it up by.

@Entity(name="user")
@dataclass
class UserV2:
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str

Registering under a name that's already taken

Entity names are unique. If both User and UserV2 above are defined, the second one decorated raises ValueError at decoration time, naming both classes, because both claim "user". Give one of them a different explicit name=.

docs.title: Defining Entities
docs.text: The canonical form for an Entity is a Python dataclass. Dataclasses are lightweight, require no dependencies, and work naturally with type hints.

docs.title: Simple record
docs.text:
@Entity
@dataclass
class User:
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str

docs.title: Nested structure
docs.text:
@Entity
@dataclass
class Address:
    street: str
    city: str
    country: str


@Entity
@dataclass
class Order:
    id: int
    user_id: int
    address: Address
    total: float

docs.title: Non-record data
docs.text:
Entities are not limited to database-style records. Any structured unit of data the system works with can be an entity:

@Entity
@dataclass
class Frame:
    index: int
    timestamp: float
    width: int
    height: int
    data: bytes


@Entity
@dataclass
class Reading:
    sensor_id: str
    timestamp: float
    value: float
    unit: str

docs.title: Relationship to Repository
docs.text:
An Entity describes the shape of data. A Repository manages it — storing, retrieving, and querying instances of that entity.

@Entity
@dataclass
class User:
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str


@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def get(self, user_id: int) -> User: ...

    def save(self, user: User) -> None: ...

The @Repository(User) decorator links the repository to its entity explicitly, making the relationship visible without requiring inheritance. The link requires the @Entity marker — passing a class that isn't registered with @Entity raises TypeError.

Looking up registered entities

Entity is a namespace — Entity.get("user") returns the User class (or None if unregistered), and dict(Entity.items()) returns every registered name → class pair.

docs.title: What Entity is Not
docs.text:
• Not a base class. User does not inherit from Entity. The decorator marks it; inheritance is not involved.

  • Not tied to a database. An entity represents a structured unit of data — it has no implied persistence mechanism. Where and how it is stored is the responsibility of a Repository.

  • Not a behaviour container. Entities describe data shape. Business logic belongs in a Component, Task, or Pipeline.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
Keep entities focused. An entity should represent one domain concept. If a class is growing methods and logic, consider whether that logic belongs in a Component instead.

Prefer flat structures where possible. Deeply nested entities are harder to query and pass around. If nesting grows complex, consider whether the nested type should be its own entity managed by its own repository.

Name entities after domain concepts. User, Order, Frame, Reading — not UserData, OrderRecord, or FrameObject. The entity name is the domain language.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Small, focused opendataframework projects, each isolating exactly one core abstraction, with runnable code you can read end-to-end. They live in examples/ in the repo; each has its own README.md with a full walkthrough. Read 1–9 in order — each one builds on ideas from the last.

# Example Concept(s) Docs 1 01-entity-repository/ Entity + Repository, backed by a SQLite @Component. The smallest possible data layer — no Service, no UI. Entity, Repository 2 02-component-and-context/ Two Components with a constructor dependency, showing the Context's dependency-ordered on_start()/on_stop() lifecycle. Component, Context 3 03-service/ A Heartbeat Service: setup() → run() → stop(), run() backgrounded by the framework. Deliberately not an API server. Service 4 04-task-and-pipeline/ Two Tasks composed into a Pipeline that coordinates them, run explicitly via project.context.get(...).execute(). Task, Pipeline 5 05-layer/ Components split across two Layers (@Storage, @Analytics), read back through project.context.get(cls). Layer 6 06-logger-and-view/ A Repository with an injected logger: Logger and data_view()/field() (View) — per-component logging and self-describing data representation. Logger, View 7 07-config-environments/ Same app/ code, two config directories (config/dev/, config/prod/) — no environment flag, just a different path. Config 8 08-function/ Plain functions made framework-aware with Function: called by key through project.context.call(...) with an injected @Component, injected into a @Task, and still callable directly, unchanged. Function 9 09-agent/ A Librarian Agent: handed a question through project.context.call(...), it works towards an answer step by step, acting on an injected @Component. The model is a rule-based stand-in — no provider, no API key. Agent

Every example is self-contained: config.toml (or a config/ directory) plus an app/ package, runnable with python main.py from inside the example's own directory. None of them add third-party dependencies beyond opendataframework itself and the Python standard library.

Looking for the CLI, UI, MCP, or chat?

Those, and the full DataView catalog, are out of scope here on purpose — see the odf package's own examples/ instead, which depends on opendataframework and demonstrates that surface.

Why no Namespace or Project example

Namespace and Project appear as supporting cast throughout every example above (every main.py uses Project; every decorator is built on Namespace), so a standalone example would mostly repeat what's already shown.

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
A Function is a plain Python function made known to the framework. It is to a function what a Component is to a class: registered and wired through dependency injection, with no execution contract of its own.

It exists for adoption. An existing codebase written as functions can become framework-aware one decorator at a time, without a class refactor first — the function itself, its callers, and its tests stay exactly as they were.

Functions answer one question:

How do I bring the code I already have into the framework?

docs.title: When to use Function
docs.text:
Use @Function when:

  • you are adopting the framework in an existing, function-based project
  • a piece of logic is stateless and a class would add nothing but ceremony
  • you want a function to be callable by name with arguments — by a UI, a CLI, or an MCP server built on top of the framework

Prefer a class — Component, Task, Service — as soon as the logic needs state or startup and shutdown hooks. @Function is the on-ramp; classes remain the recommended shape for code written for the framework from the start.

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Function decorator registers the function into the Function namespace under the kebab-case form of its name. The function is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Function
def load_data(path: str) -> list[dict]: ...

Registered as load-data.

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
@Function(name="loader")
def load_data(path: str) -> list[dict]: ...

Only functions can be decorated

Applying @Function to a class raises TypeError at decoration time, as does a callable with no name of its own (a functools.partial, an instance with __call__). A function already wrapped by another decorator, such as functools.cache, is fine. The reverse holds too: @Component, @Task and the other execution types raise on a function and point here.

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
A function is tagged with a Layer the way a class is — layer outermost:

@Storage
@Function
def load_data(path: str, db: Postgres) -> int: ...

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
A class separates its dependencies (__init__) from its arguments (the method). A function has one signature for both, so the Context splits it by type — the same rule it applies to constructors:

  • a parameter annotated with a type the Context manages is injected
  • every other parameter is a call argument, supplied by the caller
@Component
class Postgres: ...


@Function
def load_data(path: str, db: Postgres, limit: int = 100) -> int: ...

Here db is injected and becomes an edge in the dependency graph; path and limit are what a caller passes.

A parameter whose type the framework doesn't manage is simply an argument, whatever it is:

@Function
def score(model: SklearnModel, threshold: float, db: Postgres) -> float: ...

model and threshold are call arguments; only db is injected.

A parameter annotated Logger receives a Logger bound to the function's own name, as it would for a class.

String annotations are not injected

As with constructors, only an annotation that is an actual type counts. Under from __future__ import annotations every annotation is a string, so nothing is injected and every parameter stays a call argument. The same holds for a class that asks for a function (see Injecting a Function). Calling such a function through the Context without the argument raises a TypeError that names the string annotation as the cause; remove the import (or the quotes) to have it injected.

docs.title: Calling a Function
docs.text: There are three ways to call a registered function. Only the first existed before you added the decorator, and it is unaffected by it.

docs.title: Directly
docs.text:
load_data("data.csv", db=fake_db)

Nothing is injected, wrapped, or logged — every argument is passed by the caller. This is why existing callers and tests keep working unchanged.

docs.title: By key, through the Context
docs.text:
project.context.call("function.load-data", path="data.csv")  # db injected

call() takes the function's key, function.<name> (in any casing — "function.load-data" or "function.load_data"), and its remaining arguments as keywords. It is the counterpart of execute() for a Task, with the one difference that a function takes arguments. This is what a caller holding only a key and a payload uses.

docs.title: By function, through the Context
docs.text:
load = project.context.get(load_data)  # db already filled in
load("data.csv")
load("data.csv", limit=10)

get() returns the function with its managed dependencies bound. Positional arguments fill the remaining parameters in order, so an injected parameter that happens to come first doesn't shift them.

The bound function describes itself the same way: its signature leaves the injected parameters out, while its name and docstring are the original's.

inspect.signature(load)  # (path: str, limit: int = 100) -> int

So it can be handed as is to anything that builds a schema from a callable — an McpTool handler, or a tool for an agentic library — and only the parameters a caller can supply are asked for.

Both forms follow the same rules:

  • An explicit argument wins. Passing db=fake_db to call() or to the bound function overrides the injected value.
  • A missing argument fails clearly. If a required parameter is neither managed nor supplied, a TypeError names it and its type: score() is missing 'model' (SklearnModel) — not managed by the Context and not supplied by the caller.
  • Calls are logged. Start, completion with duration, and any exception go to the function's own log, like execute() on a Task.

Both become usable once project.start() returns, and raise KeyError for a function the Context hasn't resolved.

docs.title: Injecting a Function
docs.text:
Project code rarely calls a function by name. A class that needs one declares it in its constructor, like any other dependency, and calls it in its own logic. Since a function is not a type, the annotation names it through Annotated:

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Annotated


@Function
def low_stock(inventory: Inventory, threshold: int = 5) -> list[str]: ...


@Task
class Reorder:
    def __init__(self, find_shortages: Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], low_stock]):
        self.find_shortages = find_shortages

    def execute(self) -> list[str]:
        return self.find_shortages(threshold=3)  # inventory is already filled in

The annotation has two halves:

  • Callable[..., list[str]] is what the class receives, as a type checker sees it
  • low_stock is which registered function to inject — the part the Context reads

What arrives is the same callable project.context.get(low_stock) returns: the function with its own managed dependencies bound, every call logged. Reorder never mentions Inventory. The parameter name is free, as it is for a class dependency, and any class the Context creates can ask this way — a Component, a Task or Pipeline, a Service, an Agent — as can another function.

The function joins the dependency graph: it is bound after the types it takes and before the classes that ask for it, and a cycle through it is reported like any other (see Context).

docs.title: Typing the callable
docs.text:
The first half describes the function minus the parameters the Context injects, and is written by hand — Python has no way to derive it. Two spellings are useful:

Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], low_stock]  # any arguments, checked return type
Annotated[Callable[[int], list[str]], low_stock]  # checked arguments too

Callable[[int], ...] cannot express a default or a keyword, so a type checker would reject find_shortages() and find_shortages(threshold=3) even though both work. Use ... when callers rely on either.

To keep constructors short, define the annotation once next to the function:

LowStock = Annotated[Callable[..., list[str]], low_stock]


@Task
class Reorder:
    def __init__(self, find_shortages: LowStock): ...

A type LowStock = ... alias works the same way.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The constructor takes any callable, so a test needs no framework:

def test_reorder():
    assert Reorder(lambda threshold: ["bolts"]).execute() == ["bolts"]

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
A script-style module, before:

def restock(inventory, item, quantity):
    inventory.stock[item] = inventory.stock.get(item, 0) + quantity
    return inventory.stock[item]

After — one decorator, and a type on the parameter the framework should supply:

@Component
class Inventory:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.stock: dict[str, int] = {}


@Function
def restock(inventory: Inventory, item: str, quantity: int) -> int:
    inventory.stock[item] = inventory.stock.get(item, 0) + quantity
    return inventory.stock[item]

project.start()
project.context.call("function.restock", item="apple", quantity=10)

Existing calls such as restock(inventory, "apple", 10) still work as written.

docs.title: Inspecting Functions
docs.text:
project.context.functions maps every resolved function to its bound callable. It is separate from project.context.instances, which holds classes only.

project.context.parameters(func) returns the parameters a caller must supply — the signature minus whatever the Context injects — as inspect.Parameter objects:

project.context.parameters(load_data)
# → {"path": <Parameter "path: str">, "limit": <Parameter "limit: int = 100">}

This is what tooling uses to build a form or a tool schema for a function without re-implementing the injection rule.

docs.title: What Function is Not
docs.text:
• Not stateful, and without a lifecycle. There is no instance, and no on_start()/on_stop(). State belongs in a component the function takes as a parameter.

  • Not a Task. A Task has an execute() contract and takes no arguments. A function has no contract and does take arguments. The Context cannot run one on its own — it doesn't know the arguments — so a function is not itself a step of a Pipeline; a task that injects it is.

  • Not async. The Context calls and never awaits, so a registered async def function makes project.start() raise TypeError. Keep an async function out of @Function and call it yourself, or make it synchronous.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: I need to... Use Provide a reusable capability Component Run a process indefinitely Service Execute a bounded unit of work once, no arguments Task Call a unit of work with arguments Function Make an existing function known to the framework Function Call a registered function from a class Inject it with Annotated Coordinate multiple tasks into a workflow Pipeline Work towards a goal handed over at call time Agent Manage persistent data Repository

docs.title: Layer
docs.text:
A Layer is an architectural grouping that organises components at the organisational level. It answers one question:

Which subsystem does this belong to?

Layers separate concerns at the organisational level — Api, Storage, Analytics, Messaging — without affecting how components are wired or executed. A component's layer and its execution type (Component, Repository, Service, Task, Pipeline, Agent) are independent concepts.

docs.title: Two Roles
docs.text:
Layer plays two roles in the framework:

As a user-facing decorator — applied to a class or function to declare which subsystem it belongs to. This is what most application code interacts with.

@Analytics
@Task
class MetricsFetcher: ...


@Analytics
@Function
def score(model: Model, threshold: float) -> float: ...

A layer tags something that is already registered, so it always goes on top — see What a Layer accepts.

As a framework concept — a Namespace subclass in its own right, providing structured access to the components it contains via <Layer>.items()/<Layer>.get(name).

docs.title: Built-in Layers
docs.text:
The framework ships with a set of common pre-defined layers:

Layer Typical contents Api API servers, request handlers, validators Storage Databases, file systems, caches Analytics Models, pipelines, metric collectors Messaging Queues, brokers, event buses Monitoring Health checks, loggers, tracers Security Auth handlers, token validators

Built-in layers are pre-defined @Layer classes — there is no special treatment for them. They follow the same rules as any custom layer.

docs.title: Defining a Layer
docs.text: A layer is a Namespace subclass registered with @Layer. The class inherits from Namespace so that it can act as a decorator for the components that belong to it.

docs.title: Without a name — framework derives it
docs.text:
@Layer
class MachineLearning(Namespace): ...

The framework converts the class name automatically

MachineLearning is registered under the kebab-case form machine-learning — but .get() normalizes its argument, so all three forms below find the same entry:

Layer.get("machine-learning")  # kebab-case — the registered key itself
Layer.get("machine_learning")  # snake_case
Layer.get("MachineLearning")   # PascalCase — the original class name

See Name Derivation below for the full picture, including the config key convention.

docs.title: With an explicit name — use when the derived name isn't what you want
docs.text:
@Layer("ml")
class MachineLearning(Namespace): ...

Now the layer is looked up as Layer.get("ml") instead of Layer.get("machine-learning"). Use explicit names when brevity or a domain convention matters more than the derived default.

docs.title: Using a Layer Decorator
docs.text:
The layer decorator is stacked above the execution type decorator. Layer comes first (outermost), execution type second:

@Storage
@Service
class Postgres: ...


@Analytics
@Task
class MetricsFetcher: ...


@Api
@Component
class Validator: ...

The name identifying a component within its layer belongs on the execution type decorator — not the layer. The layer says where it belongs; the execution type says what it is and optionally what it is called:

@Api
@Service("users-api")
class UsersApi: ...


@Analytics
@Task("metrics-fetcher")
class MetricsFetcher: ...

docs.title: Name Derivation
docs.text:
The framework applies the same automatic name derivation to both layers and execution types. Given a class name, the framework produces:

Class name snake_case (also accepted by .get()) Registered name (kebab-case) MachineLearning machine_learning machine-learning UsersApi users_api users-api MetricsFetcher metrics_fetcher metrics-fetcher Postgres postgres postgres

.get() normalizes any of these forms to kebab-case before lookup, so Layer.get("machine_learning") and Layer.get("machine-learning") both resolve. For an execution type, the registered name is the second half of the class's key, <namespace>.<name> (service.users-api), which also names its config section — see Config structure convention.

An explicit name on the decorator overrides the derived name entirely:

@Layer("ml")
class MachineLearning(Namespace): ...


# → Layer.get("ml")  (not Layer.get("machine-learning"))

docs.title: Custom Layers
docs.text:
Custom layers follow exactly the same pattern as built-in layers:

@Layer
class MachineLearning(Namespace): ...


@MachineLearning
@Component
class Classifier: ...


@MachineLearning
@Task
class ModelTrainer: ...


@MachineLearning
@Pipeline
class TrainPipeline: ...

Accessible by class through the resolved Context, or by name through the layer namespace itself:

project.context.get(Classifier)
project.context.get(ModelTrainer)
project.context.get(TrainPipeline)

MachineLearning.get("classifier")  # → Classifier
dict(MachineLearning.items())  # → {"classifier": Classifier, ...}

docs.title: What a Layer accepts
docs.text:
A layer is an organisational tag, not a registration of its own: it accepts a class that an execution type (@Component, @Service, @Task, ...) has registered, or a function registered with @Function. Anything else raises TypeError at decoration time:

@Storage
class Warehouse: ...  # TypeError — no execution type under it


@Storage
def load_data(): ...  # TypeError — no @Function under it


@Component
@Storage
class Warehouse: ...  # TypeError — the layer runs first and finds nothing registered

The fix is the same each time: put the execution type (or @Function) directly on the class or function, and the layer above it.

A class and a function tagged with the same layer share its names, so LoadData and load_data collide there as load-data; give one an explicit name (@Storage(name=...)).

docs.title: Inspecting Layer Membership
docs.text:
Two lookup directions are available, depending on what you know:

Layer.get(name) — given a kebab-case name, return the layer class:

Layer.get("storage")  # → Storage
Layer.get("analytics")  # → Analytics
Layer.get("unknown")  # → None

<layer>.get(name) — given a component name, return the component class:

Storage.get("postgres")  # → Postgres
Analytics.get("metrics-fetcher")  # → MetricsFetcher

Together, the two-level namespace hierarchy gives structured access without any reverse-lookup machinery:

dict(Layer.items())  # → {"api": Api, "storage": Storage, …}
dict(Storage.items())  # → {"postgres": Postgres, …}
dict(Analytics.items())  # → {"metrics-fetcher": MetricsFetcher, …}

docs.title: Layer is Independent of Config
docs.text:
Layer has no bearing on config structure. Config sections are keyed by <namespace>.<name> — the execution type and the name — regardless of which layer (if any) a component belongs to — see Config structure convention:

[service.users-api]
host = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8080

[service.postgres]
database_url = "postgresql://localhost/mydb"

[task.metrics-fetcher]
source_url = "https://api.example.com/metrics"

[component.classifier]
model_path = "models/classifier.pkl"

Seeing layers in practice

The sibling odf package's UI groups components by their Layer when displaying them — a "Storage" section, an "Analytics" section, and so on. That's just today's one consumer, though — Layer.get(name) lookups work the same whether or not anything is reading them for display.

docs.title: Layer and Execution Type are Independent
docs.text:
The layer describes where a component belongs. The execution type describes how it participates in the system. Any combination is valid:

@Storage
@Service
class Postgres: ...


@Analytics
@Task
class MetricsFetcher: ...


@Api
@Component
class Validator: ...


@Api
@Pipeline
class UserOnboarding: ...


@Service
class Scheduler:
    # no layer — belongs directly to the Context
    ...

A component tagged with a layer is registered in both the execution type namespace and the layer namespace — two independent views of the same class:

Service.get("postgres")  # → Postgres  (execution type view)
Storage.get("postgres")  # → Postgres  (layer view)

docs.title: What Layer is Not
docs.text:
• Not an execution contract. A layer does not define what methods a component implements. That is determined by the execution type (Service, Task, etc.).

  • Not a base class. Components do not inherit from their layer. The decorator marks membership; inheritance is not involved.

  • Not required. A component without a layer decorator is managed directly by the Context and accessible via project.context.get(cls) just like any other component. Layers are organisational — they are not needed for DI or lifecycle management to work.

  • No protocol on the layer-defining class. class MachineLearning(Namespace): ... inherits from Namespace so that @MachineLearning works as a decorator. The class body is always empty — there is nothing to implement. Classes tagged with a layer follow their execution type's protocol (Service, Task, Agent, ...); the layer itself adds only organisational membership.

docs.title: Logger
docs.text: Logger is a per-component logging handle. It is declared as a constructor dependency exactly like any other — logger: Logger — but the Context resolves it differently from everything else: instead of handing out one shared instance, every consumer receives its own Logger, already bound to its own <namespace>.<name> key, so self.logger.info(...) needs no name argument and still lands in that component's own log file.

docs.title: Declaring it
docs.text:
from opendataframework import Logger, Task


@Task
class ExportUsers:
    def __init__(self, users: Users, logger: Logger) -> None:
        self.users = users
        self.logger = logger

    def execute(self) -> None:
        self.logger.info("export starting")
        ...

Four levels are available, each writing one line to the component's own log file:

self.logger.debug("...")
self.logger.info("...")
self.logger.warning("...")
self.logger.error("...")

Only components that want to log explicitly need to declare it — omit the parameter if you have nothing to say.

See examples/06-logger-and-view/ for a full runnable project built around this.

docs.title: Automatic Logging
docs.text:
Most log lines require no code at all. Context writes to each component's log file on its behalf:

  • Resolution — "Users resolved" (the class or function's own name), once each component is instantiated or each Function is bound.
  • Lifecycle — setup()/run()/stop() for a Service, on_start()/ on_stop() for a Component/Repository — start, completion, and any raised exception.
  • Execution — execute() for a Task/Pipeline, invoke() for an Agent, every call of a Function made through the Context — start, duration, and any raised exception.

logger: Logger is only needed for messages specific to what a component is actually doing — the framework-level lifecycle noise above is covered either way.

docs.title: Enabling File Logging
docs.text:
Log files are written under a single directory, one <namespace>.<name>.log per registered class or function — the same key the Context addresses it by, so @Task class Loader and @Agent class Loader never share a file — scoped to one Context. Project.from_config/from_dict enable it automatically under [project] log-dir (default "logs", relative to the current working directory):

[project]
log-dir = "logs"

Constructing a Context directly without a log_dir disables file logging entirely: writes become no-ops and reads return nothing.

docs.title: Reading Logs Back
docs.text:
Context.tail_logs(key, lines=300) returns the most recent entries for a component, oldest first:

project.context.tail_logs("service.postgres", lines=100)
# → [{"ts": "2026-08-08 10:00:00", "level": "INFO", "message": "setup() starting"}, ...]

Seeing it in practice
