The sibling odf package's UI's per-component log panel is backed by this same method, via GET /api/components/{component_id}/logs.

docs.title: Not a Singleton — Special-Cased Resolution
docs.text:
Every other registered class (Component, Service, Task, Pipeline, Agent, Repository) is a per-Context singleton: Context creates exactly one instance and stores it under that class in Context.instances, which is what project.context.get(cls) looks up (see Context).

Logger doesn't fit that model, so it isn't registered in any namespace and never gets a slot in Context.instances at all. Instead, Context detects a logger: Logger constructor parameter directly and supplies a fresh Logger bound to the consuming class's own name. A Context with ten components that all declare logger: Logger has ten live Logger instances, each writing to a different file; there is no single canonical one.

Practically, this means:

project.context.get(Logger)  # doesn't work — no canonical instance to return

There's no equivalent lookup for Logger — it only exists bound to whichever class asked for it via its own constructor.

docs.title: What Logger is Not
docs.text:
• Not resolvable via context.get(Logger). Logger is never registered in a namespace or given a slot in Context.instances, so there's no single shared instance to fetch.

  • Not a global or process-wide logger. Each Context owns its own set of log files, with nothing shared implicitly across Project instances. Nothing stops two Projects configured with the same log_dir from writing to the same files, though — keeping log_dir distinct per Project is up to you.

  • Not enabled by default outside Project.from_config/from_dict. A bare Context() has no log_dir, so logging is a no-op unless one is passed explicitly.

docs.title: Namespace
docs.text:
Namespace is the base class for all framework decorator types. Subclassing it produces a named scope — a decorator that registers user-defined classes and functions under a name → object mapping and exposes that mapping for inspection.

Entity, Component, Repository, Service, Task, Pipeline, Agent and Layer are all Namespace subclasses. Function is one too — the one that registers functions rather than classes. Each maintains its own independent mapping, and each says what it may be applied to — see What each decorator accepts.

docs.title: When to use Namespace
docs.text:
Namespace is a framework extension point, not an end-user concept. Inherit from it when adding a new first-class decorator type to the framework — a new kind of managed object that the Context should be aware of.

End users work with the concrete subclasses (@Component, @Service, etc.) and never interact with Namespace directly.

docs.title: Defining a Namespace
docs.text:
Subclassing Namespace is all that is required. Each subclass automatically receives its own empty _namespace dict at definition time:

from opendataframework.namespace import Namespace


class Component(Namespace): ...


class Service(Namespace): ...

Both decorators are now independent. Registering a class with @Component does not appear in Service._namespace.

docs.title: Decorator protocol
docs.text: Every Namespace subclass supports two decoration styles out of the box.

docs.title: Bare decorator
docs.text:
@Component
class Classifier: ...

The class is registered under the kebab-case form of its name, classifier. The class itself is returned unchanged — no base class is added, no methods are injected.

docs.title: Factory decorator
docs.text:
@Component(name="metrics-classifier")
class Classifier: ...

The class is registered under the explicit name. Again, the class is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text:
Namespace exposes two class methods for reading the mapping:

Component.get("Classifier")  # → Classifier, or None
Component.get("metrics-classifier")  # → Classifier registered under a custom name

dict(Component.items())  # → {"classifier": Classifier, ...}

These are used by the Context at startup to discover registered classes and build the dependency graph. Application code does not call them directly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each Namespace subclass carries its own _namespace dict — assigned automatically via __init_subclass__ when the subclass is defined. It is never shared between sibling subclasses.

The dual-use decorator protocol is implemented through __new__ and __call__:

  • Bare usage — __new__ detects a class or function argument, writes directly into _namespace, and returns it. Instance creation is bypassed entirely.
  • Factory usage — __new__ returns a Namespace instance; __init__ stores the explicit name; __call__ writes into _namespace when the instance is applied to the class.

Duplicate names raise

Registering two objects under the same name within one Namespace subclass raises ValueError, naming both — whether the collision comes from two bare decorators (two classes or functions that happen to kebab-case to the same name), two factory decorators with the same explicit name=, or one of each. This happens at definition time (when the decorator runs), not at Context/Project start time. Rename one of them, or give one an explicit name=.

docs.title: Names are unique per namespace, keys everywhere
docs.text:
Uniqueness is checked within one Namespace subclass only, so the same name can be registered in several: a @Task class Loader, an @Agent class Loader and a @Function def loader coexist. Each object also has exactly one name in a namespace — registering it twice under different names raises ValueError.

Together that makes <namespace>.<name> unique, and it is what the Context addresses everything by — "task.loader", "agent.loader", "function.loader" — and what each log file is named after. qualified(Task, "loader") builds a key and parse("Task.Loader") normalizes one; both live in opendataframework.namespace.

docs.title: What each decorator accepts
docs.text:
A plain Namespace subclass registers any named class or function. The framework's own decorators are narrower, and each raises TypeError at decoration time — in both the bare and the factory form — when applied to something else:

Decorator Accepts A plain Namespace subclass A class, or a named function @Component, @Repository, @Service, @Task, @Pipeline, @Agent A class that has no other execution type @Entity A class @Function A function @Layer A Namespace subclass A layer (@Storage, a custom one, ...) A class or function that is already registered

Three consequences worth knowing:

@Component
def load_data(): ...  # TypeError — to register a function, use @Function


@Component
@Task
class Refresh: ...  # TypeError — a class takes one execution type


@Storage
class Warehouse: ...  # TypeError — a layer tags what an execution type registered

An execution type says how the Context treats a class, so a class carries exactly one. A Layer is an organisational tag on top of that, which is why it goes outermost and why it has nothing to tag on a bare class or function.

Component and Function are separate namespaces, so a class LoadData and a function load_data can coexist — each is load-data in its own mapping. Tagged with the same layer they would collide there, as two same-named classes do.

Type checkers

A type checker accepts a function under any of these decorators, because the function overload is declared once, on Namespace. @Component def f is therefore caught when the module is imported rather than in the editor.

docs.title: What Namespace is Not
docs.text:
• Not an end-user API. Application code uses @Component, @Service, etc. Namespace is for framework contributors adding new decorator types.

  • Not a global registry. Each subclass owns its mapping independently. There is no single registry that spans all types — Context reads from each namespace separately.

  • Not inherited by user classes. Classifier does not inherit from Component or Namespace. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
A Pipeline is an executable that coordinates multiple Tasks — and optionally other Pipelines — into a single, ordered workflow. Wired through dependency injection the same way as a Component, it represents the execution flow of a data process from start to finish.

Pipelines answer one question:

In what order does the work happen?

Unlike a Task, a Pipeline does not perform work itself. It delegates to the tasks and pipelines it depends on, defines the order they run in, and optionally aggregates their results.

docs.title: When to use Pipeline
docs.text:
Use @Pipeline when a process consists of multiple steps that need to run in sequence or depend on each other's results.

Typical examples:

  • ETL workflows
  • daily analytics runs
  • model training workflows
  • deployment pipelines
  • ML experiment pipelines

If the work is a single bounded step, use Task instead.

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Pipeline decorator registers the class into the Pipeline namespace as an executable orchestration component. The Context reads from this namespace at startup. The class is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics: ...

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
@Pipeline(name="daily-analytics")
class DailyAnalyticsIngestAndReportingPipeline: ...

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
@Analytics
@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics: ...

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
A Pipeline implements a single method — execute(). It may return a value or None.

@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics:
    def execute(self):
        # coordinate tasks and sub-pipelines
        # return a result, or None
        ...

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Tasks and sub-pipelines are declared as constructor dependencies. The Context resolves and injects them automatically — including their own dependencies.

@Analytics
@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics:
    def __init__(
        self,
        fetcher: MetricsFetcher,
        trainer: ModelTrainer,
        report: ReportGenerator,
    ):
        self.fetcher = fetcher
        self.trainer = trainer
        self.report = report

    def execute(self):
        self.fetcher.execute()
        self.trainer.execute()
        self.report.execute()

docs.title: Composing Pipelines
docs.text:
A Pipeline can depend on other Pipelines the same way it depends on Tasks — through the constructor. This allows complex workflows to be built from smaller, reusable pipelines.

@Analytics
@Pipeline
class IngestPipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        fetcher: MetricsFetcher,
        validator: Validator,
    ):
        self.fetcher = fetcher
        self.validator = validator

    def execute(self):
        data = self.fetcher.execute()  # also saved to Metrics by the task itself
        self.validator.validate(data)


@Analytics
@Pipeline
class TrainPipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        trainer: ModelTrainer,
        report: ReportGenerator,
    ):
        self.trainer = trainer
        self.report = report

    def execute(self):
        self.trainer.execute()
        self.report.execute()


@Analytics
@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics:
    def __init__(
        self,
        ingest: IngestPipeline,
        train: TrainPipeline,
    ):
        self.ingest = ingest
        self.train = train

    def execute(self):
        self.ingest.execute()
        self.train.execute()

Each sub-pipeline is independently testable and reusable across other pipelines.

fit() mutates the one shared Classifier instance

TrainPipeline's trainer: ModelTrainer internally calls self.classifier.fit(data) — see the Full Example below for its body. Context creates exactly one Classifier instance for the whole application lifetime (see Component), so that call mutates the single shared instance, not a private copy. Anything else Classifier is injected into (a prediction task, an API endpoint) sees the same, now-fitted object.

Passing a step's result on

A pipeline can use a task's return value however it likes, because its execute() is plain Python. It can pass the value to a Function or a component method, as IngestPipeline does with self.validator.validate(data). It can't pass the value to another task, because a task's execute() takes no arguments (see Task, Function or Agent?). When one task needs another's output, the first task saves it where the second one reads it: MetricsFetcher saves to Metrics, and ModelTrainer loads from it. That also keeps each task runnable on its own by key, without the steps before it.

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
A complete analytics pipeline wiring together fetch, train, and report steps — including the Tasks it coordinates, in full:

@Analytics
@Task
class MetricsFetcher:
    def __init__(self, config: Config, metrics: Metrics):
        self.config = config.task.metrics_fetcher
        self.metrics = metrics

    def execute(self):
        data = self._fetch(self.config.source_url)
        self.metrics.save(data)
        return data

    def _fetch(self, url): ...


@Analytics
@Task
class ModelTrainer:
    def __init__(self, config: Config, classifier: Classifier, metrics: Metrics):
        self.config = config.task.model_trainer
        self.classifier = classifier
        self.metrics = metrics

    def execute(self):
        data = self.metrics.load(self.config.training_dataset)
        self.classifier.fit(data)


@Analytics
@Task
class ReportGenerator:
    def __init__(self, config: Config, metrics: Metrics):
        self.config = config.task.report_generator
        self.metrics = metrics

    def execute(self):
        data = self.metrics.load(self.config.report_period)
        report = self._build(data)
        self._export(report, self.config.output_path)
        return report

    def _build(self, data): ...

    def _export(self, report, path): ...


@Analytics
@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics:
    def __init__(
        self,
        fetcher: MetricsFetcher,
        trainer: ModelTrainer,
        report: ReportGenerator,
    ):
        self.fetcher = fetcher
        self.trainer = trainer
        self.report = report

    def execute(self):
        self.fetcher.execute()
        self.trainer.execute()
        return self.report.execute()

Running it through the Context, by its key:

result = project.context.execute("pipeline.daily-analytics")

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
PipelineProtocol documents the expected interface and is available for type checking and introspection:

from opendataframework import PipelineProtocol

isinstance(instance, PipelineProtocol)  # True if execute() is present

PipelineProtocol is @runtime_checkable. The Context uses it to verify that a registered class implements execute() before calling it.

class PipelineProtocol(Protocol):
    def execute(self): ...

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text: Failure handling within a pipeline is not defined by the framework at this stage. If a step raises an exception, it propagates naturally. Hooks for logging, retrying, or aggregating results across steps may be introduced in a future version.

docs.title: What Pipeline is Not
docs.text:
• Not a task. A Pipeline does not perform work itself — it delegates to tasks and sub-pipelines. If the work is a single step, use Task.

  • Not a scheduler. A Pipeline executes when called. Scheduling — running it on a timer or trigger — is the responsibility of a Service such as a Scheduler.

  • Not a base class. DailyAnalytics does not inherit from Pipeline. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: I need to... Use Provide a reusable capability Component Run a process indefinitely Service Execute a bounded unit of work once, no arguments Task Call a unit of work with arguments Function Coordinate multiple tasks into a workflow Pipeline Work towards a goal handed over at call time Agent Manage persistent data Repository

docs.title: Project
docs.text: The Project is the composition root of the framework. It owns the Context and is the single entry point for starting and stopping the application.

docs.title: From a config file
docs.text:
The primary way to create a Project is from a config file:

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")

docs.title: From a config directory
docs.text:
For larger projects, config can be split across multiple files in a directory. The framework merges them into a single configuration:

project = Project.from_config("config/")

A typical config directory might look like:

config/
├── storage.toml
├── analytics.toml
├── api.toml
└── data.toml

docs.title: From a dict
docs.text:
For programmatic use — testing, tooling, dynamic configuration:

project = Project.from_dict(
    {
        "repository": {
            "users": {
                "table": "users",
                "schema": "public",
            },
        },
        "service": {
            "postgres": {
                "database_url": "postgresql://localhost/mydb",
            },
        },
    }
)

docs.title: Pointing at the app package
docs.text:
[project] app names the module to import before the Context is built — typically your app's root package, so a hand-written import app doesn't have to sit before every Project.from_config() call:

[project]
app = "app"

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")  # imports `app` first

This doesn't scan or auto-discover anything — it's exactly one importlib.import_module() call, equivalent to writing import app yourself. Registering @Component/@Service/@Repository/@Task/ @Pipeline/@Agent classes (and @Function functions) is still the job of that module's own imports, the same way every example in this repo structures its app/__init__.py:

# app/__init__.py
from app import components, repositories, tasks

[project] app is optional — omit it and import your app package by hand before calling from_config/from_dict. A missing or broken module raises immediately (ImportError), consistent with the framework's fail-fast posture elsewhere (e.g. from_config's FileNotFoundError for a missing config path).

docs.title: Starting
docs.text:
project.start() triggers context initialisation — the dependency graph is resolved, instances are created in dependency order, and the appropriate lifecycle is applied to each component:

project.start()
    → for each component in dependency order:
        → if Service:  setup() → run() (backgrounded by framework)
        → if Component / Repository:  on_start() (blocking, return quickly)
    → blocks until all components are initialised
    → returns — everything is ready

After project.start() returns, every component's setup()/on_start() has completed — the framework blocks on each in dependency order and waits for it to return before moving on. There's no hidden latency on first access as long as components do their readiness work there: opening connections, running migrations, allocating resources. A Service's run() is only launched in the background by this point, not waited on — see Service for what belongs in each stage.

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")
project.start()

# everything ready immediately
users = project.context.get(Users).all()
project.context.get(DailyAnalytics).execute()

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
project.stop() tears down all components in reverse dependency order:

project.stop()
    → for each component in reverse dependency order:
        → if Service:  stop() (signals background thread to exit, waits)
        → if Component / Repository:  on_stop() (blocking, return quickly)
    → blocks until all components are stopped

project.stop()

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
After project.start(), project.context is the entry point to every resolved instance:

project.context.get(UsersApi)  # typed, by class — the common case
project.context.instances[UsersApi]  # lower-level dict access, primarily for
# framework extension authors

project.context.get(Users).all()
project.context.get(Orders).get(order_id)
project.context.get(MetricsFetcher).execute()

project.context.get(cls) resolves by class, so the return type is cls — an editor or type checker knows exactly what comes back, unlike a string-keyed lookup. See Context.

docs.title: Notebook or script
docs.text:
project.start() blocks until everything is ready, then returns control. Natural for notebooks and scripts where you want to query data or run a pipeline:

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")
project.start()

# query data
users = project.context.get(Users).all()

# run a pipeline explicitly
results = project.context.get(DailyAnalytics).execute()

project.stop()

docs.title: Long-running application
docs.text:
For a long-running application, project.start() brings up all services in the background. Something has to keep the process itself alive afterward:

project = Project.from_config("config.toml")
project.start()

Who keeps the process alive

A Service's run() executes in a daemon thread, which is torn down the instant the main thread exits — there's no blocking project.wait() today, so running this snippet on its own exits immediately and never really runs any service. Normally a launcher does this for you — the sibling odf package's CLI (odf run), for instance.

docs.title: Configuration and Environments
docs.text:
Different environments are handled by pointing to different config files or directories:

# development
project = Project.from_config("config/dev/")

# production
project = Project.from_config("config/prod/")

This keeps environment differences explicit and visible — a config file is a plain text artifact that can be read, diffed, and version-controlled without running the application.

docs.title: Multiple Projects
docs.text:
Multiple independent Project instances are supported within the same process. Each owns its own Context — there is no shared global state between them.

dev = Project.from_config("config/dev/")
prod = Project.from_config("config/prod/")

dev.start()
prod.start()

docs.title: What Project is Not
docs.text:
• Not an orchestrator. Project does not decide what runs after initialisation. Running a pipeline, querying data, or triggering a task is always triggered explicitly by application code — whether that's a top-level script, or a class that received the dependency via DI (an API handler, a scheduled job) — never something Project or Context invokes on their own.

  • Not a singleton. Multiple Project instances can coexist in the same process. Global mutable state at the framework level is avoided by design.

  • Not aware of business logic. Project owns the Context, not domain concerns. Business logic lives in components, tasks, and pipelines.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Agent: added @Agent, an execution type for goal-driven work whose steps are decided at run time — typically by a language model. An agent is a class with a single invoke() method whose signature is its author's to choose; everything it may act on is declared through its constructor like any other dependency, so it can also be injected into a Pipeline, a Service, or another agent. context.call("agent.librarian", question=...) invokes one by key, context.parameters(Librarian) returns the parameters of its invoke(), and every invocation is logged like a Task's execute(). @Agent on a class without invoke() raises TypeError at decoration time. AgentProtocol documents the interface. The framework still ships no model client and no agent loop — invoke() is where a library or provider SDK of your choice goes. See Agent.
  • Function: added @Function, a marker that makes a plain function known to the framework the way @Component does a class — so an existing function-based codebase can be adopted without a class refactor first. The function is returned unchanged, and direct calls behave exactly as before. Through the Context, parameters annotated with a managed type are injected and the rest are call arguments: context.call("function.load-data", path=...) calls by key, context.get(load_data) returns the function with its dependencies bound, context.functions lists what was resolved, and context.parameters(func) returns the parameters a caller must supply. A class — or another function — asks for one by naming it in its signature, Annotated[Callable[..., int], load_data], and receives it with its dependencies bound and its calls logged — and with a signature that leaves the injected parameters out, so it can be handed to a library that builds a tool schema from a callable; the function then takes part in dependency ordering and cycle detection. Functions have no lifecycle and aren't in context.instances. See Function.
  • View: added ContentMetadata/ContentMetadataProtocol so a Repository whose view points at content (ImageView/VideoView/AudioView/DocumentView) can declare, per record, that content's filename and content_type via an optional content_metadata(entity) method, detected structurally like DataViewProtocol/ ReplayProtocol. The values needn't be entity fields — a repository may derive them or return constants. Existing views are unchanged. Using this to label, type and offer content for download happens on the odf side. See View.
  • Layer: a function registered with @Function can now be tagged with a layer (@Storage @Function def load_data(...)), like a class. See Layer.
  • Context: a required parameter that is not injected because its annotation is a string (every annotation under from __future__ import annotations) now fails with a TypeError that names the string annotation as the cause, for a constructor and for a function called through the Context. String annotations are still not injected.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Namespace (breaking): each decorator now states what it may be applied to, and raises TypeError at decoration time otherwise. Two cases were accepted before: a class under two execution types (@Component @Task class X) — a class takes one — and a layer on a class no execution type has registered (@Storage class X, or @Component @Storage class X with the layer underneath). To migrate, keep a single execution type on the class and put the layer above it. @Component and the other execution types on a function still raise, and now point to @Function. A plain Namespace subclass accepts a function as well as a class. See Namespace.
  • Context (breaking): async is not supported, and now says so. An async def function registered with @Function, or an async def execute(), invoke(), setup()/run()/stop(), on_start()/on_stop() or repository stream method, makes project.start() raise TypeError naming it. These were previously called without being awaited — a hook that silently never ran, or a call logged as complete before it started. To migrate, make it synchronous, or keep it out of the Context and call it yourself. See Context.
  • Component (breaking): an McpTool now requires a described, fully typed handler, and raises when it is created otherwise — ValueError for an empty description, TypeError for a handler with an unannotated parameter, *args/**kwargs, no return annotation, or an annotation left as a string. A caller, typically a model, sees nothing of a tool but its description and signature, and a handler without them was accepted and offered with a schema that said little. To migrate, annotate the handler's parameters and return value (-> None counts), replace a lambda with a method or a function, and remove from __future__ import annotations from the handler's module. See Component.
  • Context (breaking): everything addressed by a string is now addressed by a key, <namespace>.<name> — execute("task.load-job"), call("agent.librarian", ...), start("service.postgres"), start_stream("repository.webcam"), tail_logs("component.cache") and the rest. The name is the registered one (kebab-case class or function name, or the explicit name=), and keys are accepted in any casing. A name is only unique within its namespace, and the bare names used before collided across them: with a @Component class Loader and a @Task class Loader, execute("Loader") could find the component and raise TypeError, a @Function and an @Agent sharing a name could not be call()ed at all, and every same-named object wrote to one log file. Now each is reachable, and log files are named <namespace>.<name>.log (logs/task.loader.log). context.key(obj) returns the key of a class or function you hold. A string without a namespace raises ValueError, and the ValueError call() raised for a function and an agent sharing a name is gone. To migrate, prefix every name passed to the Context with its namespace, and point anything reading log files at the new names. See Context.
  • Namespace (breaking): registering one object under two names in the same namespace (@Task("a") @Task("b") class X) now raises ValueError, so every object has exactly one key. See Namespace.
  • Repository (breaking): @Repository(...) now requires its argument to be a class registered with @Entity, and raises TypeError at decoration time otherwise. The docs always described the argument as the Entity class, but any class was accepted — so @Repository written directly above the repository class (entity left out) took that class for its own entity, registered nothing, and left the repository silently missing from the Context. To migrate, add @Entity to the entity class; for a type you don't own, call Entity(SomeType) once or wrap it in a small entity class. See Repository.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Context: a class that declared the same dependency under two constructor parameters (def __init__(self, source: Db, target: Db)) failed at project.start() with a misleading Circular dependency detected among: Sync. It still fails — the Context holds a single Db, so both parameters would receive the same object — but now with a ValueError that says so and names the class, the dependency and the parameters.
  • Config: key normalisation only applied to the name being looked up, not to the keys in the data, so a key written as exclude_years (or ExcludeYears) in TOML couldn't be found by any access path. config.exclude_years and config["exclude_years"] raised, and config.get("exclude_years", default) silently returned the default. Config now normalises its keys to kebab-case on construction (recursively through nested tables), so snake_case/kebab-case/PascalCase are interchangeable on both sides. Two keys in the same table that normalise to the same name (e.g. exclude_years and exclude-years) now raise ValueError instead of one silently shadowing the other. See Config.
  • Namespace: applying a decorator (@Component, @Task, @Service, ...) to a function instead of a class registered nothing and raised nothing — the bare form silently rebound the function's name to a namespace instance, and the factory form registered the function as if it were a class. Both now raise TypeError at decoration time, naming the namespace and the offending object. @Repository applied directly to a function (entity left out) raises the same way. See Namespace.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• Config sections in the docs and examples now follow a class's key: a @Service class Postgres reads [service.postgres] as config.service.postgres, instead of a flat [postgres]. The section, the Context key and the log file now share one name, and same-named classes in different namespaces no longer share a section. This is a convention, not a Config change — any structure still works. See Config.
  • A Task's execute() takes no arguments, by design, and the docs no longer suggest giving it an optional parameter to receive the previous step's result, as the 0.2.0 notes did. Work whose input the caller decides is a Function; a value that differs per deployment is config, and one that follows from earlier runs is state kept in a repository. A pipeline passes a task's result on to a function or a component method, not to another task. See Task, Function or Agent?.
  • Corrected pages that had fallen behind 0.3.0: Entity no longer says a duplicate name silently overwrites (it has raised since 0.2.0), Agent and Component describe how a server such as odf's offers agents and functions as tools without mcp_tools(), and Service examples read their own config section.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Project: Project.from_dict() now imports the module named under [project] app (if present) before constructing the Context — equivalent to writing import app by hand before calling from_config()/from_dict(). from_config() gets this for free since it delegates to from_dict(). Fails fast on a missing/broken module (ImportError propagates uncaught). See Project.
  • Config: Config.get() and Config[] now run the key through normalize(), same as __getattr__, so snake_case/kebab-case/PascalCase are interchangeable on every access path — including looking a section up by its class-derived name (e.g. config.get("Postgres") for a [postgres] TOML section). See Config.
  • Component: added McpTool/McpToolsProtocol so a Component can expose its own MCP tools via an optional mcp_tools() method, detected structurally like DetailsProtocol/ChartProtocol. Wiring this into an actual MCP server happens on the odf side. See Component.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Namespace: registering two classes under the same name (via kebab-casing or an explicit name) used to silently overwrite the earlier registration. Both registration paths now raise ValueError naming both colliding classes. See Namespace.
  • Config: Config.__init__ previously stored the given dict by reference, so mutating the original dict after passing it to Project.from_dict() would silently leak through — contradicting the documented read-only/immutable contract. Config now owns a deep copy instead. See Config.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • View: renamed ReplayProtocol.replay_field to field, aligning with the generic field/fields naming convention used by every other View variant. See View.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• Clarified that a Task's execute() can already accept an optional parameter to receive the previous step's return value directly within a Pipeline's own execute() — no framework change needed, just previously undocumented. The only fixed zero-arg contract is Context.execute(name), the external CLI/UI/MCP entry point. See Pipeline.
  • Fixed the Startup/Shutdown Order diagrams in Context, which mislabeled Config as a Component. Config isn't decorated with @Component and is pre-seeded before resolution starts, so Lifecycle never iterates over it.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
A Repository manages Entities. It abstracts persistence and data access concerns away from business logic — components, tasks, and pipelines ask the repository for data without needing to know where it comes from or how it is stored.

Repositories answer one question:

Where does the data come from?

The rest of the system should not need to know.

docs.title: When to use Repository
docs.text:
Use @Repository when a class is responsible for:

  • querying and retrieving entities
  • persisting or updating entities
  • abstracting a data source — a database, an external API, a file, a stream

Typical examples:

  • a database table wrapper
  • an external API client that returns structured data
  • a file reader that produces records
  • a cache layer over another repository

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text:
The @Repository decorator takes the Entity class it manages as an argument. This makes the relationship between repository and entity explicit and visible.

@Repository(User)
class Users: ...

The entity must be an @Entity

The argument has to be a class registered with @Entity; anything else raises TypeError at decoration time. This also catches the entity being left out — @Repository written directly above the repository class would otherwise take that class for its own entity, register nothing, and leave the repository silently missing from the Context. To manage a type you don't own, register it explicitly with Entity(SomeType), or wrap it in a small entity class of your own.

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
@Repository(User, name="users")
class Users: ...

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users: ...

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
A Repository has no strictly required methods — only the operations relevant to the data source need to be implemented. The following are conventional starting points.

opendataframework.repository exposes runtime_checkable protocols — ReadableProtocol, WritableProtocol, and StreamableProtocol — so tooling can detect these capabilities via isinstance() without requiring every repository to implement all of them:

from opendataframework.repository import ReadableProtocol, StreamableProtocol, WritableProtocol

isinstance(users, ReadableProtocol)  # True if `all()` is implemented
isinstance(users, WritableProtocol)  # True if `save()` and `delete()` are implemented
isinstance(webcam, StreamableProtocol)  # True if `stream()` is implemented

@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def get(self, user_id: int) -> User:
        # retrieve a single entity by identifier
        ...

    def all(self) -> list[User]:
        # retrieve all entities
        ...

    def save(self, user: User) -> None:
        # persist a new or updated entity
        ...

    def delete(self, user_id: int) -> None:
        # remove an entity by identifier
        ...

Not all repositories need all four. A read-only data source implements only get() and all(). A write-only sink implements only save().

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Some data sources are live and unbounded — a webcam feed, a sensor reading queue, a subscription to a message topic. all() doesn't fit: there's no "every record", only entities arriving for as long as something keeps listening. stream() is the repository's answer to that case:

from opendataframework.repository import StreamableProtocol


@Storage
@Repository(Frame)
class Webcam:
    def stream(self) -> Iterator[Frame]:
        while True:
            frame = self._read_next_frame()
            yield frame

StreamableProtocol is independent of ReadableProtocol/WritableProtocol — a repository can be streamable only, readable only, or any combination. Detected the same way:

isinstance(webcam, StreamableProtocol)  # True if `stream()` is implemented

StreamableProtocol only drives lifecycle, not display

StreamableProtocol only drives the stream's lifecycle — the background thread, and whether start_stream()/stop_stream() are allowed. It says nothing about how the UI should display what comes out of stream(). That's a separate, optional declaration — see View's StreamingVideoView/StreamingAudioView.

docs.title: Starting and stopping a stream
docs.text:
Unlike all() or get(), which run once when called, a stream is something that gets explicitly started and stopped — the Context drives one background thread per repository that iterates stream() and fans each entity out to every current subscriber, so multiple consumers share a single running feed instead of each triggering an independent call to stream().

Two more, both optional, hooks bracket that background thread's lifetime:

@Storage
@Repository(Frame)
class Webcam:
    def __init__(self, config: Config):
        self.device = config.repository.webcam.get("device", 0)
        self.capture = None

    def open_stream(self):
        # blocking; called once, right before the background thread starts
        self.capture = self._open_device(self.device)

    def close_stream(self):
        # called once the background thread has fully exited — whether that's
        # because streaming was stopped, the source ended on its own (e.g. the
        # device disconnected), or stream() raised
        self.capture.release()
        self.capture = None

    def stream(self) -> Iterator[Frame]:
        while True:
            ok, image = self.capture.read()
            if not ok:
                break
            yield self._encode(image)

open_stream()/close_stream() are not the same as on_start()/on_stop() (see below): on_start()/on_stop() run once, for the whole Project's lifetime. open_stream()/close_stream() run every time streaming is started and stopped, which may happen many times over the Project's life — they tie an expensive resource (a camera handle, a socket) to the stream actually being active, not to the process being up. A repository streaming from an already-open resource (a queue, a socket handed in via the constructor) needs neither hook.

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Like all components, a Repository declares its dependencies through the constructor. The Context resolves and injects them automatically.

@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
    ):
        self.config = config.repository.users
        self.connection = None

    def on_start(self):
        self.connection = self._connect(self.config.database_url)

    def on_stop(self):
        self.connection.close()

    def get(self, user_id: int) -> User: ...

    def save(self, user: User) -> None: ...

    def _connect(self, url): ...

docs.title: Database repository
docs.text:
@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
    ):
        self.config = config.repository.users
        self.connection = None

    def on_start(self):
        self.connection = self._connect(self.config.database_url)

    def on_stop(self):
        self.connection.close()

    def get(self, user_id: int) -> User:
        row = self.connection.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", user_id)
        return User(**row)

    def all(self) -> list[User]:
        rows = self.connection.query("SELECT * FROM users")
        return [User(**row) for row in rows]

    def save(self, user: User) -> None:
        self.connection.execute(
            "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO users VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            user.id,
            user.name,
            user.email,
        )

    def delete(self, user_id: int) -> None:
        self.connection.execute("DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?", user_id)

    def _connect(self, url): ...

docs.title: Read-only external source
docs.text:
Not all repositories write. An external API or data stream may be read-only:

@Storage
@Repository(Reading)
class SensorFeed:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
    ):
        self.config = config.repository.sensor_feed
        self.client = None

    def on_start(self):
        self.client = self._connect(self.config.feed_url)

    def on_stop(self):
        self.client.disconnect()

    def get(self, sensor_id: str) -> Reading:
        raw = self.client.fetch(sensor_id)
        return Reading(**raw)

    def all(self) -> list[Reading]:
        raw = self.client.fetch_all()
        return [Reading(**r) for r in raw]

    def _connect(self, url): ...

docs.title: Live streaming feed
docs.text:
A repository can be stream-only too — no get()/all()/save() at all, just a live feed, with open_stream()/close_stream() tying the device to the stream's own start/stop rather than the whole Project's lifetime:

@Storage
@Repository(Frame)
class Webcam:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
    ):
        self.device = config.repository.webcam.get("device", 0)
        self.capture = None

    def open_stream(self):
        self.capture = self._open_device(self.device)

    def close_stream(self):
        self.capture.release()
        self.capture = None

    def stream(self) -> Iterator[Frame]:
        while True:
            ok, image = self.capture.read()
            if not ok:
                break
            yield self._encode(image)

    def _open_device(self, device): ...

    def _encode(self, image): ...

docs.title: Using a repository in a Task
docs.text:
@Analytics
@Task
class MetricsFetcher:
    def __init__(
        self,
        feed: SensorFeed,
        metrics: Metrics,
    ):
        self.feed = feed
        self.metrics = metrics

    def execute(self):
        readings = self.feed.all()
        for reading in readings:
            self.metrics.save(reading)
        return readings

docs.title: What Repository is Not
docs.text:
• Not a service. A Repository manages data access — it does not run indefinitely or manage an execution environment. If the data source requires a long-running process, that process is a Service that the repository depends on. A stream() implementation is still just an iterator — the background thread that keeps it running and fans it out to subscribers is the framework's concern, not the repository's; the repository author never manages threading directly.

  • Not a base class. Users does not inherit from Repository. The decorator registers it and links it to its entity; inheritance is not involved.

  • Not responsible for business logic. A repository retrieves and persists entities. Transforming, validating, or acting on that data belongs in a Component, Task, or Pipeline.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
One repository per entity type. A repository manages one kind of entity. If you find a repository managing two unrelated entities, split it.

Keep queries in the repository. Filtering, sorting, and pagination belong in the repository — not in the components that use it. Components should ask for what they need, not receive everything and filter themselves.

Read-only repositories are valid. Not every data source supports writes. A repository that only implements get() and all() is a complete and legitimate design.

Streaming is orthogonal, not a replacement. stream() doesn't replace get()/all() — a repository can be readable, writable, streamable, or any combination, since each capability is detected independently via its own protocol.

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
A Service is a long-running executable — wired through dependency injection the same way as a Component, but with a mandatory setup → run → stop lifecycle the Context drives automatically. It represents a runtime capability that the framework starts and keeps alive for the duration of the application.

Services answer one question:

What needs to keep running?

Note: Service here means an executable runtime capability, not a business-logic layer some other frameworks name that way. Think process, server, or worker — not UserService or OrderService.

docs.title: When to use Service
docs.text:
Use @Service when a class needs to:

  • start up and run indefinitely until explicitly stopped
  • manage an execution environment (a server, a container, a connection pool)
  • expose a long-lived capability to the rest of the application

If the work is finite and runs to completion, use Task or Pipeline instead.

Typical examples:

  • API servers
  • database processes
  • message queue workers
  • schedulers
  • workers that feed an Agent
  • Docker containers

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Service decorator registers the class into the Service namespace as a long-running executable component. The Context reads from this namespace at startup. The class is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Without arguments
docs.text:
@Service
class Postgres: ...

docs.title: With a name
docs.text:
@Service("postgres")
class PostgresConnectionPoolManager: ...

docs.title: Combined with a Layer
docs.text:
@Storage
@Service
class Postgres: ...

@Api
@Service
class UsersApi: ...

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
A Service follows a three-stage lifecycle managed by the framework:

setup → run → stop
Method Purpose Blocking setup() Blocking setup — pull images, run migrations, open connections Yes run() Block and serve — runs for the lifetime of the application Yes* stop() Release resources, close connections, shut down gracefully Yes

Why run() is marked Blocking* but doesn't stall startup

run() is blocking by nature — the framework automatically spawns it in a background thread so startup can continue to the next component. The service author does not need to manage threading.

All three methods must be defined. Stages with no work can be left as pass (or ...).

docs.title: Framework-Managed Concurrency
docs.text:
The framework knows that run() will block. It handles this automatically:

project.start()
    → setup()     ← blocking, framework waits
    → run()       ← framework spawns in background thread, continues to next component

The service author implements run() as a plain blocking call. Threading is never the service's responsibility.

@Storage
@Service
class Postgres:
    def setup(self): ...

    def run(self):
        self.pool.serve()  # blocks — framework handles the thread

    def stop(self): ...

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
@Service
class Postgres:
    def setup(self):
        # blocking setup: pull image, run migrations, open connection pool
        # framework waits for this to return before proceeding
        ...

    def run(self):
        # block and serve for the lifetime of the application
        # the framework spawns this in a background thread automatically
        ...

    def stop(self):
        # signal run() to exit and release resources gracefully
        # example: close connections, flush buffers, shut down server
        ...

docs.title: on_start() vs setup()
docs.text:
Service uses setup(), run(), and stop() — not the on_start() / on_stop() hooks used by Component and Repository. This is intentional:

  • The framework needs to know which method to background — it can only do that with an explicit contract.
  • on_start() is a lightweight initialisation hook expected to return quickly. setup() is the place for heavier blocking work: pulling images, running migrations, opening connection pools.

A Service may still define on_start() / on_stop() if it has lightweight concerns separate from the service lifecycle, but the primary lifecycle is setup → run → stop.

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Like all components, a Service declares its dependencies through the constructor:

@Storage
@Service
class Postgres:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
    ):
        self.config = config.service.postgres
        self.pool = None

    def setup(self):
        self._pull_image(self.config.image)
        self.pool = self._create_pool(self.config.database_url)
        self._run_migrations()

    def run(self):
        self.pool.serve()

    def stop(self):
        self.pool.close()

    def _pull_image(self, image): ...

    def _create_pool(self, url): ...

    def _run_migrations(self): ...

docs.title: API server
docs.text:
@Api
@Service
class UsersApi:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
        users: Users,
    ):
        self.config = config.service.users_api
        self.users = users
        self.server = None

    def setup(self):
        self.server = self._create_server(self.config)
        self.server.bind(self.config.host, self.config.port)

    def run(self):
        self.server.serve()

    def stop(self):
        self.server.shutdown()

    def _create_server(self, config): ...

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta


@Service
class Scheduler:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
        pipeline: DailyAnalytics,
    ):
        self.config = config.service.scheduler
        self.pipeline = pipeline
        self._running = False

    def setup(self):
        self._running = True

    def run(self):
        while self._running:
            self._wait_for_next_run()
            if self._running:
                self.pipeline.execute()

    def stop(self):
        self._running = False

    def _wait_for_next_run(self):
        # block until the next scheduled run, e.g. once a day at 02:00
        now = datetime.now()
        next_run = now.replace(hour=self.config.get("hour", 2), minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
        if next_run <= now:
            next_run += timedelta(days=1)

        # sleep at most 60s at a time, re-checking _running after each nap,
        # so stop() is noticed within a minute rather than only after
        # a single sleep() covering the whole (possibly ~24h) gap
        while self._running and datetime.now() < next_run:
            remaining = (next_run - datetime.now()).total_seconds()
            time.sleep(min(60, remaining))

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
ServiceProtocol documents the expected interface and is available for type checking and introspection:

from opendataframework import ServiceProtocol

isinstance(instance, ServiceProtocol)  # True if all three lifecycle methods are defined

ServiceProtocol is @runtime_checkable. The Context uses isinstance to distinguish services from components and then calls all three lifecycle stages unconditionally.

from opendataframework import ServiceProtocol


class ServiceProtocol(Protocol):
    def setup(self) -> None: ...
    def run(self) -> None: ...
    def stop(self) -> None: ...

docs.title: What Service is Not
docs.text:
• Not a business logic container. A Service manages a runtime capability, not domain logic. Business logic belongs in a Component, Task, or Pipeline that the Service depends on.

  • Not responsible for its own threading. run() should block naturally. The framework spawns it in a background thread and manages concurrency automatically.

  • Not a base class. Postgres does not inherit from Service. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: I need to... Use Provide a reusable capability Component Run a process indefinitely Service Execute a bounded unit of work once, no arguments Task Call a unit of work with arguments Function Coordinate multiple tasks into a workflow Pipeline Work towards a goal handed over at call time Agent Manage persistent data Repository

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
A Task is a finite executable — wired through dependency injection the same way as a Component, but with a single execute() contract the Context calls once. It represents a bounded unit of work that runs once, produces a result, and completes. Unlike a Service, it does not run indefinitely. Unlike a Pipeline, it does not coordinate other tasks.

Tasks answer one question:

What work needs doing, once?

docs.title: When to use Task
docs.text:
Use @Task when a class needs to:

  • perform a single, well-defined unit of work
  • optionally produce a result
  • run to completion and stop

Typical examples:

  • fetching data from an external source
  • generating a report
  • training or evaluating a model
  • sending a notification
  • exporting data to storage

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text: The @Task decorator registers the class into the Task namespace as a finite executable component. The Context reads from this namespace at startup. The class is returned unchanged.

docs.text:
A Task implements a single method — execute(). It may return a value or None.

@Task
class MetricsFetcher:
    def execute(self):
        # perform the work
        # return a result, or None if the task has only side effects
        ...

class MetricsFetcher:

        self.metrics.save(data)

    def _fetch(self, url): ...

docs.title: Using a Task
docs.text:
A Task is resolved and executed through the Context, by its key:

data = project.context.execute("task.metrics-fetcher")

Or directly within a Pipeline that coordinates multiple tasks:

@Pipeline
class DailyAnalytics:
    def __init__(
        self,
        fetcher: MetricsFetcher,
        trainer: ModelTrainer,
        report: ReportGenerator,
    ):
        self.fetcher = fetcher
        self.trainer = trainer
        self.report = report

    def execute(self):
        self.fetcher.execute()
        self.trainer.execute()
        return self.report.execute()

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
TaskProtocol documents the expected interface and is available for type checking and introspection:

from opendataframework import TaskProtocol

isinstance(instance, TaskProtocol)  # True if execute() is present

TaskProtocol is @runtime_checkable. The Context uses it to verify that a registered class implements execute() before calling it.

class TaskProtocol(Protocol):
    def execute(self): ...

docs.title: Task, Function or Agent?
docs.text:
The Context can run all three by key. What separates them is who decides the input:

Who decides the input Use Run with Nobody at call time: it is fixed when the project is assembled, through the constructor and Config Task context.execute(key) The caller, on every call Function context.call(key, **kwargs) The caller, who hands over a goal; the steps are decided at run time Agent context.call(key, **kwargs)

execute() takes no arguments on purpose. Because a task needs nothing from its caller, anything can run it (a pipeline, a scheduler, the CLI, a UI) without knowing anything about it. A task that took arguments would be a function written as a class, and choosing between the two would come down to taste.

docs.title: When the work needs per-run input
docs.text:
Sooner or later a task wants a value that changes between runs, such as the day to backfill or the tenant to reprocess. Don't change Config at run time or set a module-level variable to get it there. Both are hidden dependencies, and the second is global state. Instead, choose by where the value comes from:

  • The caller picks it each time. The work is a Function. A task can still cover the usual case by injecting the function and passing the value itself:

    @Function
def backfill_orders(orders: Orders, day: date) -> int: ...


@Task
class DailyOrders:
    def __init__(self, backfill: Annotated[Callable[[date], int], backfill_orders]):
        self.backfill = backfill

    def execute(self) -> int:
        return self.backfill(date.today() - timedelta(days=1))

    project.context.execute("task.daily-orders")  # the scheduled run: yesterday
project.context.call("function.backfill-orders", day=date(2026, 10, 1))  # a one-off

  • It differs per deployment or environment. It's configuration. Start the project from a different config path (see Config).

  • It follows from what earlier runs did, such as a watermark, a cursor or the last day processed. It's state. Keep it in a Repository that the task reads at the start of execute() and updates at the end.

docs.title: What Task is Not
docs.text:
• Not called with arguments. execute() takes none, and Context.execute() passes none. Work that needs input from its caller is a Function; see Task, Function or Agent?.

  • Not a long-running process. A Task runs to completion. If the work needs to run indefinitely, use a Service.

  • Not an orchestrator. If the work involves coordinating multiple tasks, use a Pipeline.

  • Not required to return a value. execute() may return None when the task produces only side effects — saving to storage, sending a notification, writing a file.

  • Not a base class. MetricsFetcher does not inherit from Task. The decorator registers it; inheritance is not involved.

docs.title: View
docs.text:
A Repository may optionally implement data_view() to say two things about its data: which kind of representation fits it — a name, like TableView, LocationView, DocumentView — and which field(s) on the entity are the ones worth looking at. That's all it is: a small piece of self-describing metadata a repository attaches to itself.

opendataframework has zero third-party dependencies and renders nothing itself — data_view() doesn't draw a table or open a map, it just answers the question a renderer would need answered:

Given a repository that already exposes data somehow, what's the single best representation of one of its records, and which field(s) does that representation hinge on?

Seeing it in practice

If you're running a project through odf's UI, data_view() is what that UI reads to decide how a repository's data shows up when you open it — as a table, a map, a video player, and so on. That's just today's one consumer, though: the declaration is metadata a repository carries regardless of whether odf — or anything else — is reading it.

This is independent of ReadableProtocol/WritableProtocol/ StreamableProtocol (see Repository) — those still gate whether the underlying operation (all()/save()/delete()/stream()) is actually allowed. data_view() never decides that; it only describes which single representation best fits the data once it's already accessible.

See examples/06-logger-and-view/ for a full runnable project built around this.

docs.title: Why a single view
docs.text:
A repository picks exactly one view — there is no mixing. A repository whose data is best shown on a map doesn't also carry a raw-table representation of the same records; the map's marker popups already show every field. This keeps each repository's self-description unambiguous: one capability, one representation.

A consumer may still offer a table fallback

"Exactly one view" is about what a repository declares — a consumer is still free to layer a fallback on top. The sibling odf package's UI does this for LocationView/TimeseriesView: alongside the declared map or timeline, it offers a one-click toggle to the same plain table that any readable dataclass-entity repository gets by default when it implements no data_view() at all (see below). That toggle isn't a second data_view() — the repository still declared one view — it's the consumer choosing to render that declaration two ways.

docs.title: The default: table
docs.text:
A repository doesn't need to implement data_view() at all. A ReadableProtocol repository with a dataclass entity is represented as a plain table by default — every field as a column, in declaration order:

@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def all(self) -> list[User]: ...
    def save(self, user: User) -> None: ...
    def delete(self, user_id: int) -> None: ...

Users needs no data_view() — it just gets the default table, exactly as if ReadableProtocol/WritableProtocol were the only things that mattered.

A repository only implements data_view() when it wants something other than the default table, or wants to override which columns show:

from opendataframework import DataViewProtocol, TableView


@Storage
@Repository(User)
class Users:
    def all(self) -> list[User]: ...

    def data_view(self) -> TableView:
        return TableView(fields=("id", "name"))  # hide email from the table

data_view() is detected structurally via DataViewProtocol (opendataframework.view.DataViewProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required:

class DataViewProtocol(Protocol):
    def data_view(self) -> DataView: ...

docs.title: The DataView family
docs.text:
DataView is a closed set of variants, each pointing at its field(s) generically — field: str for one field, fields: tuple[str, ...] for several. The meaning comes from which variant it is, not from the attribute name — the variant is the "view name" from the description above.

Variant Fields Typical representation Repository shape TableView fields: tuple[str, ...] \| None rows and columns (the implicit default) ReadableProtocol ImageView field: str a still image per record ReadableProtocol VideoView field: str a bounded, seekable clip per record ReadableProtocol StreamingVideoView field: str a live feed StreamableProtocol AudioView field: str a bounded, seekable clip per record ReadableProtocol StreamingAudioView field: str a live feed StreamableProtocol DocumentView field: str an arbitrary JSON-shaped value per record ReadableProtocol LocationView fields: (lat_field, lon_field) one point per record ReadableProtocol TimeseriesView field: str (the timestamp field) the entity's other numeric fields against a timestamp ReadableProtocol

Every variant except TableView needs exactly the repository capability its "Repository shape" column names — a StreamingVideoView/StreamingAudioView repository must implement stream() (StreamableProtocol) for a live representation to be meaningful at all; everything else needs all() (ReadableProtocol) to list records. How each variant actually gets rendered — a table widget, a map component, a video player — is entirely up to whatever's consuming data_view(); this package only carries the declaration.

docs.title: Location — a map, not a table
docs.text:
from opendataframework import LocationView, Repository, Storage


@Storage
@Repository(Store)
class Stores:
    def all(self) -> list[Store]: ...
    def save(self, store: Store) -> None: ...
    def delete(self, store_id: int) -> None: ...

    def data_view(self) -> LocationView:
        return LocationView(fields=("lat", "lon"))

Stores declares itself as location data, not tabular data — no separate table representation alongside it. A consumer like odf's UI turns this into one marker per record, with each record's fields available on click, the same fields that would have shown as table columns.

docs.title: Streaming video — a live feed
docs.text:
from opendataframework import Repository, Storage, StreamingVideoView


@Storage
@Repository(Frame)
class Webcam:
    def open_stream(self) -> None: ...
    def close_stream(self) -> None: ...
    def stream(self) -> Iterator[Frame]: ...

    def data_view(self) -> StreamingVideoView:
        return StreamingVideoView(field="data")

Webcam is stream-only — no all()/save(). Its data_view() names which of Frame's fields (data: bytes) holds each encoded JPEG frame; StreamableProtocol (unchanged, see Repository) is what actually drives the background thread that produces them.

docs.title: Document — arbitrary JSON, not a stringified cell
docs.text:
from opendataframework import DocumentView, Repository, Storage


@Storage
@Repository(WebhookEvent)
class WebhookEvents:
    def all(self) -> list[WebhookEvent]: ...

    def data_view(self) -> DocumentView:
        return DocumentView(field="payload")

Given WebhookEvent(id, received_at, payload: dict), this names payload as the field worth rendering as a collapsible JSON tree — instead of a consumer stringifying an arbitrary nested dict into an unreadable table cell.

docs.title: Replay — scrubbing over time
docs.text:
A repository may separately implement field() to say that its records can be scrubbed through over time, by naming which timestamp field drives that. This is independent of data_view() — a LocationView, VideoView, or AudioView repository describes what representation fits its data; field() separately says whether (and by which field) that representation can be replayed chronologically.

from opendataframework import LocationView, Repository, Storage


@Storage
@Repository(Ping)
class Pings:
    def all(self) -> list[Ping]: ...

    def data_view(self) -> LocationView:
        return LocationView(fields=("lat", "lon"))

    def field(self) -> str:
        return "recorded_at"

Pings declares both: LocationView fixes its representation as a map, and field() says the map can be scrubbed through time using recorded_at. A consumer like odf's UI turns this into a timeline scrubber alongside the map.

field() is detected structurally via ReplayProtocol (opendataframework.view.ReplayProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required, mirroring DataViewProtocol:

class ReplayProtocol(Protocol):
    def field(self) -> str: ...

A TimeseriesView repository is always replayable already — it names its own timestamp field via field — so field() only adds an affordance for LocationView/VideoView/AudioView-backed repositories. A repository with no field() simply gets no replay affordance.

docs.title: Content metadata — naming and typing the content
docs.text:
A view names the field holding the content, but says nothing about the content itself. A repository may separately implement content_metadata() to declare, for one record, what that content is called and which format it's in:

Question it answers Asked data_view() Which representation fits these records, and which field holds the content? once per repository content_metadata(entity) For this record, what is that content called, and which format is it in? once per record 
from opendataframework import ContentMetadata, ImageView, Repository, Storage


@Storage
@Repository(Photo)
class Photos:
    def all(self) -> list[Photo]: ...

    def data_view(self) -> ImageView:
        return ImageView(field="data")

    def content_metadata(self, photo: Photo) -> ContentMetadata:
        return ContentMetadata(filename=f"{photo.id}.png", content_type="image/png")

Given Photo(id, data: bytes), nothing about the file name or format is stored on the entity — Photos knows every image is a PNG and derives the name from the key. That's the point of this being a method on the repository rather than more field names on the view: the metadata often isn't business data, so it shouldn't have to become an entity field just to be declared.

When it is stored per record — an uploaded document's original name, say — the same method just reads it off the entity:

def content_metadata(self, document: Document) -> ContentMetadata:
    return ContentMetadata(filename=document.filename, content_type=document.content_type)

ContentMetadata has two attributes, both optional — return only what the repository actually knows:

Attribute Meaning filename: str \| None the content's file name, extension included (e.g. "report.pdf") content_type: str \| None the content's MIME type (e.g. "image/png")

content_metadata() is detected structurally via ContentMetadataProtocol (opendataframework.view.ContentMetadataProtocol, @runtime_checkable) — no base class or decorator required, mirroring DataViewProtocol:

class ContentMetadataProtocol(Protocol):
    def content_metadata(self, entity: object) -> ContentMetadata: ...

It only matters for a repository whose view points at content — ImageView, VideoView, AudioView or DocumentView. A repository with no content_metadata(), or one that leaves an attribute as None, simply declares nothing: a consumer is left to work the content out for itself.

A declaration, not a guarantee

Nothing in this package inspects the content, so ContentMetadata is only what the repository says about it — and the value may itself have come from somewhere untrusted, like the type a browser sent at upload. A consumer should treat it as a hint: check it against the content where it can, rely on it where it can't (nothing in the bytes tells CSV from plain text, and nothing at all carries a file name), and never let it override its own rules for what is safe to render — a declared text/html is no reason to serve markup inline. A filename needs sanitising before it goes into a header or a path.

These are facts about the content, not instructions for serving it. The two attributes line up with HTTP's Content-Disposition file name and Content-Type, but building those headers — and deciding whether content opens inline or downloads — is the consumer's job.

docs.title: What a data_view() is not
docs.text:
• Not UI code. opendataframework has zero third-party dependencies and renders nothing — data_view() is metadata a repository declares about itself, consumed by whatever renders it (today, the sibling odf package's UI). Nothing here imports or knows about odf.

  • Not a data-access capability. It never gates whether all()/save()/ delete()/stream() may be called — ReadableProtocol/WritableProtocol/ StreamableProtocol still do that, completely independent of what data_view() returns.

  • Not composable. A repository returns exactly one DataView. If a repository's data genuinely needs two different presentations, that's a sign it should be two repositories.

  • Not required. Most repositories need no data_view() at all — the implicit table default covers the common case.
